summary: Revision 2 of the GN.4 continuation, responding to the independent review. The counting plan now includes the full semialgebraic projection/measure/section/boundary chain, a lattice-based proof of triangular unipotent uniformity, and a restricted representation-pair second moment valid in the Ghosh–Sarnak range through Toma’s conductor formula. Prescribed-ball Besicovitch covers feed an explicit marked-poset theorem and the primitive-flag wedge argument. Borel density imports the existing Chevalley stabilizer and functorial representation results; the so(2,1) quotient is explicitly identified with the owner’s highest-weight-four module. Homogeneous mixing is an adapter to the base Howe–Moore theorem with its inherited proof gap. Primary-source Fourier decay and isotropic smoothing give one curvature-dependent constant over all ellipses, while the Huxley improvement remains conditional. All previous definition APIs, tests, six planets and reviewer corrections are retained; a marked-point predicate and its API/tests are added. The independent revision review accepts this finished target-level pass with the four recorded open-input groups. It adds the interval-cover adapter and corrects the Markoff, skew-counting and Siegel proof details; no formalisation or closed stage is claimed.

nodes.title: Volumes of coordinate projections
nodes.statement: Let n ≥ 1 and Z ⊆ ℝⁿ (ℝⁿ = Fin n → ℝ with Lebesgue measure). For J ⊆ Fin n let π_J : ℝⁿ → ℝ^J be the coordinate projection and V_J(Z) = vol_J(π_J(Z)) ∈ [0, ∞] its outer Lebesgue measure on ℝ^J. For 0 ≤ j ≤ n put V_j(Z) = Σ_{|J| = j} V_J(Z), with the convention V_0(Z) = 1, so V_n(Z) = vol(Z). The projection maximum of Bhargava–Shankar is Vol(Z̄) = max{V_J(Z) : 1 ≤ |J| ≤ n − 1}, which is 0 when n = 1.
hypotheses: n ≥ 1; Z arbitrary (outer measure, so no measurability is assumed). V_0 = 1 is a convention for the constant term of the error, not the measure of a point; it is used even for Z = ∅ only inside error bounds, which are then trivially true.
proofSteps: V_J is the composite of the image under the measurable linear map π_J with the outer measure on ℝ^J; V_{Fin n} = vol because π_{Fin n} is the identity up to the canonical equivalence ℝⁿ ≃ ℝ^{Fin n}.
Monotonicity, translation invariance and the scaling law |c|^{|J|} follow from the same properties of Lebesgue measure on ℝ^J and from π_J(c·Z + v) = c·π_J(Z) + π_J(v).

For an upper triangular unipotent u (u_ii = 1, u_ij = 0 for i > j) and a final segment J = {k, …, n − 1}, π_J ∘ u = u_J ∘ π_J with u_J the unipotent lower-right block, so V_J(uZ) = V_J(Z); for other J this fails (test proj_volume_shear).
acceptance: The unit cube has V_J = 1 for every J and V_j = C(n, j).
For the box [0, a] × [0, b] ⊂ ℝ²: V_1 = a + b, V_2 = ab.

nodes.title: Davenport's principle for coordinate-convex regions
nodes.statement: Let n ≥ 1, h ≥ 1 and Z ⊆ ℝⁿ compact. Suppose (1) every line parallel to a coordinate axis meets Z in the empty set or a union of at most h closed intervals (single points allowed), and (2) for every J ⊆ Fin n with 1 ≤ |J| ≤ n − 1 the projection π_J(Z) ⊆ ℝ^J has the same property for lines parallel to the axes of ℝ^J. Then |#(Z ∩ ℤⁿ) − vol(Z)| ≤ Σ_{j=0}^{n−1} h^{n−j} V_j(Z), with V_j as in coordinate-projection-volumes (V_0 = 1).
hypotheses: Compactness makes every projection compact, hence measurable, and every interval of a line section closed.
The constant is explicit; no uniformity in a family is claimed here (that is semialgebraic-interval-condition).
proofSteps: n = 1: Z is a union of at most h closed intervals I and |#(I ∩ ℤ) − len I| ≤ 1 for each.

n > 1: write N(Z) = Σ_{t∈ℤ} N(Z^{(t)}) over the slices Z^{(t)} = {y ∈ ℝ^{n−1} : (t, y) ∈ Z}. Each slice satisfies (1)–(2) in dimension n − 1, since the projections of a slice are slices of projections of Z and lines in a slice are lines in ℝⁿ; apply the induction hypothesis.

Main term: by Tonelli, Σ_{t∈ℤ} vol_{n−1}(Z^{(t)}) = ∫_{ℝ^{n−1}} #{t ∈ ℤ : (t, y) ∈ Z} dy, and the integrand differs from the length of the fibre over y by at most h, so the sum is vol(Z) + O(h·V_{n−1}-term of the projection forgetting the first coordinate).

Error terms: Σ_t V_J(Z^{(t)}) for J ⊆ {2, …, n} is again a lattice sum of slice volumes of π_{{1}∪J}(Z), estimated by the same Tonelli step; collecting the powers of h gives the stated bound (Davenport's induction, as reproduced by Barroero–Widmer).
acceptance: Z = [0, N]ⁿ with N ∈ ℕ: #(Z ∩ ℤⁿ) − vol Z = (N+1)ⁿ − Nⁿ ≤ Σ_{j<n} C(n,j) N^j, the bound with h = 1.
A finite set of h points on the x-axis in ℝ¹ has volume 0 and at most h lattice points: the bound h·V_0 = h is attained.

nodes.title: Semialgebraic sets and multisets of bounded complexity
nodes.statement: Let n, k, ℓ ∈ ℕ. A set S ⊆ ℝⁿ has description complexity at most (k, ℓ) if there are polynomials f_1, …, f_k ∈ ℝ[x_1, …, x_n] of total degree ≤ ℓ and a set Σ ⊆ {−1, 0, 1}^k of sign vectors with S = {x : (sign f_1(x), …, sign f_k(x)) ∈ Σ}. A bounded semialgebraic multiset of maximal multiplicity m and complexity (k, ℓ) is a function μ : ℝⁿ → {0, …, m} with bounded support such that each superlevel set {μ ≥ i}, 1 ≤ i ≤ m, has complexity at most (k, ℓ); its lattice count is Σ_{x∈ℤⁿ} μ(x) and its volume is ∫ μ. Every set given by a Boolean combination of at most k polynomial equalities and inequalities of degree ≤ ℓ has complexity at most (k, ℓ).
hypotheses: The sign vector set Σ is arbitrary, so complements, intersections and unions are covered without changing the polynomials.
A multiset counts lattice points with multiplicity; a set is the case m = 1.
proofSteps: Closure properties: complement replaces Σ by its complement; intersection and union of complexity (k, ℓ) and (k', ℓ') sets have complexity (k + k', max(ℓ, ℓ')).

Invertible affine changes of variables x ↦ Ax + b preserve total degree, so u(S), S − v and S/m have the same complexity; restriction to an affine subspace parametrised affinely by ℝ^d gives a set of complexity (k, ℓ) in ℝ^d.

Each complexity-(k, ℓ) set is semialgebraic (a finite Boolean combination of zero and positivity sets of polynomials); conversely a semialgebraic set has some complexity (finitely many polynomials occur in any description).
acceptance: The closed unit ball has complexity (1, 2).
A finite union of h points of ℝ has complexity (1, h).

nodes.title: Uniform bound on connected components in semialgebraic families
nodes.statement: Let S ⊆ ℝ^{m+n} be semialgebraic and for a ∈ ℝ^m let S_a = {x ∈ ℝⁿ : (a, x) ∈ S}. There is M_S ∈ ℕ such that every fibre S_a is a disjoint union of at most M_S cells (in the cylindrical sense), and in particular has at most M_S connected components. Consequently, for all n, k, ℓ there is B(n, k, ℓ) such that every set of complexity at most (k, ℓ) in ℝⁿ has at most B(n, k, ℓ) connected components.
hypotheses: S semialgebraic; the bound M_S depends on S only, not on a.
The consequence uses, for each of the finitely many sign-vector sets Σ ⊆ {−1,0,1}^k, the family parametrised by the coefficient vectors of k polynomials of degree ≤ ℓ.
proofSteps: Take a cylindrical decomposition of ℝ^{m+n} adapted to S (cylindrical algebraic decomposition). Its restriction to each fibre over a ∈ ℝ^m is a decomposition of ℝⁿ into at most as many cells, partitioning S_a.
Cells are connected, so S_a has at most M_S = (number of cells of the decomposition) connected components.

For the consequence: the set {(c, x) : x lies in the complexity-(k, ℓ) set with coefficient vector c and sign set Σ} is semialgebraic in ℝ^{N+n}, N the number of coefficients; take B = the maximum of the M_S over the finitely many Σ.
acceptance: For k = 1, ℓ = 2 in ℝ¹ (sets {sign(ax² + bx + c) ∈ Σ}) every such set has at most 3 components.
The fibres of S = {(a, x) : x² < a} are empty or one interval: M_S = 1 suffices for the component count.

nodes.title: Davenport's interval condition for semialgebraic regions
nodes.statement: For fixed n, k, ℓ there is h(n,k,ℓ) such that every set Z ⊆ ℝⁿ with complexity at most (k,ℓ), each of its coordinate projections, and every axis-parallel line section of those projections have at most h connected components (intervals, allowing points and open or half-open endpoints). More generally, for a fixed semialgebraic family Z ⊆ ℝ^{m+n} there is h_Z working simultaneously for every linear image Ψ(Z_T), every parameter T, and all its coordinate projections.
hypotheses: Linear maps Ψ are unrestricted and need not be invertible. No fibre-volume function or iterated superlevel family is part of this assertion.
proofSteps: Encode the coefficients of Ψ and the parameter T in W={(Ψ,T,y): ∃x, (T,x)∈Z and y=Ψx}. This is a single semialgebraic family by projection closure; its description does not change with Ψ.

For each coordinate set J and axis i∈J, encode the remaining fixed coordinates of the line as more parameters. Apply semialgebraic-uniform-components to the resulting family of subsets of ℝ. There are only finitely many choices of J,i; take the maximum of their bounds.

For bounded complexity, use a universal coefficient family of k polynomials of degree at most ℓ and a sign selector. A selector is a subset of the finite set {−1,0,1}^k, so finitely many universal families suffice. The maximum of their constants depends only on n,k,ℓ.
acceptance: For the open unit disc in ℝ² every axis-parallel line section is one interval and each projection is (−1, 1): h = 1 works.
For a set of complexity (1, ℓ) in ℝ¹, h = ℓ + 1 works.

sources.locator: §4 'The Davenport constant', p.13, and Corollary 3.13, p.12 (arXiv:1210.5943)
sources.match: Shows that a definable family has a uniform Davenport constant: the number of connected components of the intersection of a line with a projection of a fibre is uniformly bounded; this lemma is the semialgebraic case with the bound depending on (n, k, ℓ).

sources.locator: Proposition 2.5 and the paragraph after it, physical p.14
sources.match: Asserts that Davenport's argument applies to bounded semialgebraic multisets with a constant depending only on (n, m, k, ℓ); the interval condition is the input that makes this so.

nodes.title: Davenport's estimate for triangular unipotent images
nodes.statement: For n≥1 and k,ℓ∈ℕ there is C(n,k,ℓ) such that for every bounded semialgebraic Z⊆ℝⁿ of complexity at most (k,ℓ) and every upper or lower triangular unipotent real matrix u, |#(uZ∩ℤⁿ)−vol(Z)| ≤ C(n,k,ℓ) Σ_{j=0}^{n−1} V_j(Z). The volumes are those of Z. For a semialgebraic multiset with multiplicity at most m and with each multiplicity superlevel set of complexity at most (k,ℓ), the same estimate holds with constant m C(n,k,ℓ) and the corresponding sum of projection volumes of those sets.
hypotheses: No integrality of u is needed. The multiplicity-zero exterior is excluded from the superlevel decomposition.
proofSteps: Put Λ=u⁻¹ℤⁿ. Its covolume is one and x↦ux is a bijection Z∩Λ→uZ∩ℤⁿ.

For z∈ℤⁿ nonzero, choose its last nonzero coordinate i when u is upper triangular. The i-th coordinate of u⁻¹z equals the nonzero integer z_i, since all subsequent z_j vanish. Thus ‖u⁻¹z‖∞≥1 and ‖u⁻¹z‖₂≥1. Every Euclidean successive minimum of Λ is therefore at least one. For lower triangular u use the first nonzero coordinate.

Apply semialgebraic-family-lattice-count to Z and Λ. For each sign selector use the universal polynomial-coefficient family intersected with a closed Euclidean ball whose radius is another parameter. All fibres of this enlarged family are bounded, as BW Theorem 1.3 requires; every bounded complexity-(k,ℓ) set occurs unchanged by taking a sufficiently large radius. There are finitely many sign selectors, so the maximum constant depends only on n,k,ℓ. Drop the minima denominators, which are at least one. No fibre-volume function is integrated.

For a multiset, sum the estimate over the m nonempty multiplicity superlevel sets. This also proves the base packet’s Bhargava–Shankar multiset clause after bounding the finite projection sum by a dimension constant times max(1, largest proper coordinate projection volume).
acceptance: u = identity recovers davenport-principle up to the constant.

n=2, 0≤ε≤1, T≥0, Z=[0,ε]×[0,T], u(x,y)=(x+ay,y): each integer y gives at most two integer x, hence the count is at most 2(⌊T⌋+1) for every a. This is within C(1+ε+T), although the first projection of uZ can have length ε+|a|T.

sources.locator: Proposition 2.5 and following paragraph, physical p.14
sources.match: The asserted triangular unipotent estimate is recovered with the original projection volumes. The proof here uses a different route and makes no source-error claim.
The lattice-uniform theorem applied to u⁻¹ℤⁿ, together with the elementary last-coordinate argument, gives the estimate.

nodes.title: Lattice points in a ball, by successive minima
nodes.statement: Let Λ is a discrete subgroup of a finite-dimensional real inner-product space E, of rank R ≥ 1, viewed as a full lattice in V = span_ℝ Λ with its induced inner product; λ_1 ≤ … ≤ λ_R are its successive minima for the closed unit ball of V (GN.1 successive-minimum, one-based here) and det Λ its covolume in V. Then for every T > 0, #(Λ ∩ B̄(0, T)) ≤ 2^{3R−1}·Σ_{j=0}^{R} T^j/(λ_1⋯λ_j), the j = 0 term being 1. In particular #(Λ ∩ B̄(0, T)) ≤ 2^{3R−1}(R + 1)·max_{0≤j≤R} T^j/(λ_1⋯λ_j).
hypotheses: No lower bound on T is needed; for T < λ_1 the count is 1 and only the j = 0 term matters.
The constant is explicit; the ambient dimension of E plays no role.
proofSteps: Transport Λ isometrically to a full lattice in ℝ^R (GN.1 successive-minimum-linear-equiv); the minima are unchanged.
Apply Henk Theorem 1.5 (pp.2–3) with its ceiling factors: for R ≥ 2 the count is < 2^{R−1}∏_i ceil(2T/λ_i + 1). For R = 1 use the direct interval count ≤ 1 + 2T/λ_1.

Since ceil(2x+1) ≤ 2(1+x) for x ≥ 0, expand the product. For each subset I of size j, ∏_{i∈I} λ_i ≥ λ_1⋯λ_j; hence the bound is ≤ 2^{2R−1}Σ_j binom(R,j)T^j/(λ_1⋯λ_j) ≤ 2^{3R−1}Σ_j T^j/(λ_1⋯λ_j). The rank-one interval bound also satisfies the displayed estimate.
acceptance: Λ = ℤ^R, T = 1: the count is 2R + 1 and the bound is 2^{3R−1}(R + 1).
Λ = aℤ with a > 2T: the count is 1, the j = 0 term.

sources.locator: Lemma 3.5, first bound, p.9 (arXiv:2006.02356v1), citing Schmidt, Duke Math. J. 35 (1968), Lemma 2
sources.match: The count of lattice points of a rank-R lattice in a ball of radius T ≥ 1 is ≪_R Σ_i T^{R−i}/(λ_1⋯λ_{R−i}).
The product bound used in the proof, with explicit constant.

sources.locator: Proposition 5.2, p.23 (author copy dated 4 April 2025); arXiv v1 p.21
sources.match: The same estimate for a bounded domain, quoted from Schmidt; see bounded-domain-count.

nodes.title: Ball count past an intermediate minimum
nodes.statement: Let Λ is a discrete subgroup of a finite-dimensional real inner-product space E, of rank R ≥ 1, viewed as a full lattice in V = span_ℝ Λ with its induced inner product; λ_1 ≤ … ≤ λ_R are its successive minima for the closed unit ball of V (GN.1 successive-minimum, one-based here) and det Λ its covolume in V. If 1 ≤ i₀ ≤ R and T ≥ λ_{i₀}, then #(Λ ∩ B̄(0, T)) ≤ C_R·T^R/(λ_1⋯λ_{i₀−1}·λ_{i₀}^{R−i₀+1}), with C_R = 2^{3R−1}(R + 1).
hypotheses: T ≥ λ_{i₀} is required: for smaller T the right-hand side can be smaller than 1.
proofSteps: Start from ball-count-successive-minima. For j ≤ i₀ − 1 bound T^j/(λ_1⋯λ_j) by T^R/(λ_1⋯λ_{i₀−1}λ_{i₀}^{R−i₀+1}) using T ≥ λ_{i₀} ≥ λ_i (i ≤ i₀); for j ≥ i₀ use λ_i ≥ λ_{i₀} for i ≥ i₀.
Sum the R + 1 terms.
acceptance: i₀ = R: the bound reads T^R/(λ_1⋯λ_R) ≍ T^R/det Λ, the volume order.
i₀ = 1: T^R/λ_1^R.

sources.locator: Lemma 3.5, second bound and its proof, pp.9–10
sources.match: For i₀ ∈ {1, …, R} and T ≥ λ_{i₀}, the count is ≪_R T^R/(λ_1⋯λ_{i₀−1}λ_{i₀}^{R−i₀+1}).

nodes.title: Schmidt's count in a dilated bounded domain
nodes.statement: Let Λ be a lattice of rank k in ℝ^m with Euclidean successive minima μ_1 ≤ … ≤ μ_k, and D ⊆ ℝ^m bounded. There is C = C(k, D) with #(Y·D ∩ Λ) ≤ C·max_{0≤j≤k} Y^j/(μ_1⋯μ_j) for every Y > 0; the j = 0 term is 1. Without the j = 0 term the bound is false whenever 0 ∈ D: the origin is always counted while every other term tends to 0 as Y → 0.
hypotheses: The j = 0 term is necessary: for 0 ∈ D the origin is always counted.
proofSteps: Choose r with D ⊆ B̄(0, r); then #(YD ∩ Λ) ≤ #(Λ ∩ B̄(0, rY)).
Apply ball-count-successive-minima and bound (rY)^j by max(1, r)^k Y^j.
acceptance: Λ = ℤ^k, D = (−1, 1)^k, Y → 0: the count is 1 = the j = 0 term while every other term tends to 0.

sources.locator: Proposition 5.2, p.23 (author copy dated 4 April 2025); arXiv v1 p.21
sources.match: States the bound with the maximum over 1 ≤ j ≤ k; the corrected range 0 ≤ j ≤ k is PAPER-BHARGAVA-SHANKAR-WANG-25/E14 (confirmed).
The ball case.

nodes.title: Counting vectors of bounded norm in a definite quadratic lattice
nodes.statement: Let (L, Q) be a free ℤ-module of rank r ≥ 1 with a positive definite quadratic form Q (real-valued). Let μ_i = inf{y > 0 : L contains i linearly independent vectors v with Q(v) ≤ y²} and a_i = μ_1⋯μ_i (a_0 = 1), as in GN.1 successive-minimum-partial-product. Then for every Y > 0, #{v ∈ L : Q(v) ≤ Y} ≤ 2^{3r−1}Σ_{i=0}^{r} Y^{i/2}/a_i; the nonzero count vanishes for Y < μ_1².
hypotheses: Q positive definite on L ⊗ ℝ; the minima are in the square-root normalisation of Eskin–Katznelson.
proofSteps: Give L ⊗ ℝ the inner product with ‖v‖² = Q(v); then L is a full lattice whose Euclidean minima are the μ_i.
Apply ball-count-successive-minima with T = √Y.
acceptance: L = ℤ^r with Q = sum of squares: μ_i = 1, a_i = 1 and the bound is a polynomial in √Y of degree r, matching the order Y^{r/2} of the true count.

sources.locator: §7, Definition 7.8, Lemma 7.9 and Corollary 7.10, pp.28–29; Proposition 7.11 and proof, pp.29–30 (arXiv:2011.08887v1)
sources.match: Counts vectors of bounded Q in the lattices L_n by Σ_i Y^{i/2}/a_i with a constant depending on the rank only.

sources.locator: Proof of Proposition 7.7 and footnote 32, p.37 (retrieved PDF) (arXiv:1909.07473v3)
sources.match: The count of nonzero v with Q(v) < X is ≪_r Σ_i X^{i/2}/a_i.

nodes.title: Counting nonzero vectors below the last minimum
nodes.statement: Let Λ is a discrete subgroup of a finite-dimensional real inner-product space E, of rank R ≥ 1, viewed as a full lattice in V = span_ℝ Λ with its induced inner product; λ_1 ≤ … ≤ λ_R are its successive minima for the closed unit ball of V (GN.1 successive-minimum, one-based here) and det Λ its covolume in V. Let M > 0 with M < λ_1 and Y ≥ λ_R. (a) For 0 ≤ R₀ ≤ R − 1 and 0 < T ≤ Y: #((Λ ∖ {0}) ∩ B̄(0, T)) ≤ C_R·(T^{R−R₀}Y^{R₀}/det Λ + (T/M)^{R−R₀−1}). (b) If moreover 0 ≤ j₀ ≤ R − 1, J ≥ M with J < λ_{j₀+1}, and 0 ≤ R₀ ≤ R − 1 − j₀, then #((Λ ∖ {0}) ∩ B̄(0, T)) ≤ C_R·(T^{R−R₀}Y^{R₀}/det Λ + (T/M)^{j₀}·((T/J)^{R−R₀−1−j₀} + 1)).
hypotheses: C_R depends only on R.
If T ≤ M the left side is 0, so only T > M matters.
proofSteps: (a) is (b) with j₀ = 0, J = M.

For T > M write the count via ball-count-successive-minima and split the sum at R₀: the terms with many minima use λ_{R−i+1}⋯λ_R ≤ Y^i and Minkowski's second theorem λ_1⋯λ_R ≍ det Λ; the others use λ_i > M for i ≤ j₀ and λ_i > J for i > j₀.
Sum the geometric series in T/J (T > M) as in the source.
acceptance: Λ = ℤ^R, M = 1/2, Y = 1, T = 1/4: the count is 0.
R = 1: (a) with R₀ = 0 gives a bound C(T/det Λ + 1).

sources.match: States both bounds with implied constants depending at most on R and proves them from Lemma 3.5 and Minkowski's second theorem.

nodes.title: A basis adapted to the successive minima, with coordinate bounds
nodes.statement: Let Λ be a full lattice in an R-dimensional real inner-product space E (R ≥ 1) with successive minima λ_1 ≤ … ≤ λ_R. There is a ℤ-basis b_1, …, b_R of Λ with ‖b_j‖ ≤ j·λ_j for every j, and every x = Σ_j t_j b_j ∈ E satisfies |t_j| ≤ c_R‖x‖/λ_j for every j, where c_R = 2^R·R!/V_R and V_R is the volume of the unit ball.
hypotheses: The coordinate bound holds for all real x, not only lattice points.
The basis need not realise the minima.
proofSteps: The basis comes from GN.1 basis-from-minima: b_j lies in (λ_1 + ⋯ + λ_j)·B̄, so ‖b_j‖ ≤ jλ_j.
Cramer's rule: t_j = det(b_1, …, x, …, b_R)/det(b_1, …, b_R), x in place j; Hadamard's inequality bounds the numerator by ‖x‖∏_{i≠j}‖b_i‖ ≤ ‖x‖∏_{i≠j} iλ_i.
det(b) = det Λ ≥ V_R λ_1⋯λ_R/2^R by Minkowski's second theorem; combine.
acceptance: E = ℝ^R, Λ = ℤ^R: the standard basis satisfies both bounds with t_j = x_j.
R = 1, Λ = aℤ: b_1 = a and t_1 = x/a.

sources.locator: Proofs of Lemmas 3.21 (pp.22–23) and 3.23 (p.24), citing Davenport, Proc. Roy. Soc. A 272 (1963), Lemma 5
sources.match: Uses a basis with ‖b_j‖ ≍ λ_j in which every vector x of the lattice has coordinates of size ≪ ‖x‖/λ_j.

sources.locator: §2, p.7, citing Cassels, An introduction to the geometry of numbers, Lemma 8, p.135
sources.match: A basis with |v_i| ≤ iλ_i, used to map the lattice to ℤⁿ before applying Davenport's principle.
The basis-from-minima input.

nodes.title: Widmer's lattice-point count for Lipschitz boundaries
nodes.statement: Let D ≥ 1, Λ a full lattice in ℝ^D with Euclidean successive minima λ_1 ≤ … ≤ λ_D, and S ⊆ ℝ^D bounded whose boundary ∂S is covered by the images of M maps [0,1]^{D−1} → ℝ^D, each Lipschitz with constant L (∂S is Lipschitz parametrisable in dimension D − 1 with these data). Then S is Lebesgue measurable and |#(S ∩ Λ) − vol(S)/det Λ| ≤ c₀(D)·M·max_{0≤i<D} L^i/(λ_1⋯λ_i), where the i = 0 term is 1 and c₀(D) = D^{3D²/2}.
hypotheses: The bound is uniform in Λ: it depends on Λ only through its minima, unlike the fixed-lattice count of GlobalNumberFields Layer 3.
For D = 1 the boundary is a finite set of at most M points.
proofSteps: Measurability: ∂S is a finite union of Lipschitz images of a (D−1)-cube, hence Lebesgue null.

Choose a basis with minimal orthogonality defect (adapted-basis-coordinates) and its fundamental parallelepiped P; #(S ∩ Λ) differs from vol(S)/det Λ by at most the number of translates of P meeting ∂S.

Cover each Lipschitz image by subcubes of side 1/m; each subimage has diameter ≤ L√(D−1)/m and meets a number of translates bounded by ∏_i(κL/(mλ_i) + 2) with κ the orthogonality constant; optimise m to get the maximum over i.
acceptance: Λ = ℤ^D, S = [0, N]^D: the error is (N + 1)^D − N^D ≤ c₀(D)·2D·N^{D−1}, consistent with M = 2D faces of Lipschitz constant ≍ N.
Λ = εℤ ⊕ ℤ^{D−1} with ε → 0 and S fixed: the bound grows like L/ε, the i = 1 term.

sources.locator: Theorem 5.4 and its proof, p.17 (arXiv:1204.0927; Trans. Amer. Math. Soc. 362 (2010))
sources.match: For a lattice in ℝ^D with minima λ_i and bounded S whose boundary lies in Lip(D, 1, M, L), S is measurable and the count differs from vol S/det Λ by at most c₀(D)M max_{0≤i<D} L^i/(λ_1⋯λ_i), with c₀(D) = D^{3D²/2}.
Applies Widmer's Theorem 5.4 to dilated cubes in a family of lattices Λ_g, uniformly in g.

nodes.title: Coordinate multiplicities control the measure of a smooth-stratified set
nodes.statement: For 0≤j≤n and a Borel A⊆ℝⁿ that is a countable union of C¹ submanifolds of dimension at most j, H^j(A) ≤ C_{n,j} Σ_{|I|=j} ∫_{ℝ^I} #({x∈A:π_I x=y}) dy, where counts may be infinite and the nonnegative integrals are outer integrals (ordinary Lebesgue integrals for the semialgebraic application), and H^j is Mathlib’s normalized Euclidean Hausdorff measure. One may take C_{n,0}=1 and C_{n,j}=(2√binom(n,j))^j for j>0. In particular, a semialgebraic set of dimension less than j has H^j measure zero.
proofSteps: First treat a j-dimensional C¹ manifold. At a tangent j-plane choose an orthonormal basis. Cauchy–Binet makes the sum of squares of its coordinate j-minors one, so one projection π_I has determinant at least binom(n,j)^{-1/2}. Every singular value is at most one, so the inverse differential has norm at most √binom(n,j).

The inverse function theorem and continuity give a neighborhood represented over a convex open subset of ℝ^I by an inverse section with Lipschitz constant at most 2√binom(n,j). Second countability supplies countably many such charts. Partition A into disjoint Borel pieces subordinate to them and group pieces by I.

On each piece, apply the Lipschitz image inequality to its inverse section. H^j on the coordinate plane is its Lebesgue measure by the normalization baseline. For a fixed I, summing projected-piece measures equals the integral of their multiplicity; disjointness of the original pieces bounds this by the number of points of each π_I-fibre of A. Countable additivity gives the bound. This deliberately uses a dimension constant, rather than assuming Federer’s general area formula.

For a lower-dimensional C¹ chart, exhaust its parameter domain by countably many bounded compact pieces on which its derivative is bounded. A k-dimensional box, k<j, has zero H^j content: cover it by O(δ^{-k}) cubes of diameter O(δ) and let δ→0. Lipschitz image bounds and countable unions prove nullity. At j=0 the assertion is just counting measure.
acceptance: For a j-coordinate box the only nonzero full-rank projection contributes its volume; lower-rank projections have infinite fibres on null sets, whose nonnegative integrals are zero.
A finite set has H^j=0 for j>0 and H^0 equal to its cardinality.
A sloping line segment has length bounded by a dimension constant times the sum of its two coordinate lengths.

sources.match: Identifies the needed rectifiability/coordinate-fibre measure comparison. The stated weaker dimension-constant comparison is proved here by local coordinate charts instead of importing the general Federer theorem.
Supplies smooth semialgebraic strata and agreement of dimensions through the existing owner request.

nodes.title: Uniform Hausdorff bound in families of small dimension
nodes.statement: Let S⊆ℝ^{m+n} be a fixed semialgebraic family, every fibre S_a bounded with dim S_a≤j≤n. There is c_S such that H^j(S_a) ≤ c_S Σ_{|I|=j}vol_j(π_I S_a) for every a. For j=0 use the cardinality of the finite fibre and the convention that the projection of a nonempty set to ℝ⁰ has measure one.
proofSteps: For each I the set of parameters (a,y) where the π_I-fibre has positive dimension is semialgebraic and, for fixed a, has dimension less than j by the requested fibre-dimension inequality. It has Lebesgue measure zero by the lower-dimensional clause of rectifiable-coordinate-measure-bound.

All remaining fibres are zero-dimensional semialgebraic sets, hence finite; semialgebraic-uniform-components bounds their cardinalities by one M for the single family (a,y)↦S_a∩π_I⁻¹(y). Take the maximum over the finitely many I.

Use the owner’s finite C¹ partition and the coordinate multiplicity theorem. Its right side is at most C_{n,j} M Σ_I vol(π_I S_a), since exceptional positive-dimensional fibres lie over a null set. The count of a finite zero-dimensional fibre is handled separately when j=0.
acceptance: For j=n it reduces to H^n=volume with a harmless family constant.
For j=1, n=2, a circle has length bounded by a fixed multiple of the sum of its two projection lengths.
The constant depends on the family: N parallel copies of a segment require a factor growing with N.

sources.match: The finite-fibre multiplicity argument is specialized to semialgebraic sets, with the chart-based dimension constant replacing the sharp area comparison.

nodes.title: Closures and boundaries of bounded semialgebraic fibres
nodes.statement: For a fixed semialgebraic family Z⊆ℝ^{m+n} with bounded fibres, C_T=closure Z_T and B_T=frontier Z_T form semialgebraic families with compact fibres. Each B_T has n-dimensional volume zero, vol C_T=vol Z_T, and V_j(C_T)=V_j(Z_T), while V_j(B_T)≤V_j(C_T), for 1≤j≤n. For j=0 all error-bound conventions are one.
proofSteps: Fibrewise closure and interior can be written with quantified distance inequalities; the requested owner projection/quantifier-elimination API makes the resulting families semialgebraic. A bounded fibre has compact closure.

By CAD dimension, dim frontier Z_T<n. Indeed frontier is the union of closure Z_T\Z_T and Z_T\interior Z_T; the former drops dimension, while the latter has no n-dimensional open cell. The lower-dimensional Hausdorff clause and H^n=volume give nullity and vol C_T=vol Z_T.

For any linear coordinate projection π, compactness gives π(closure Z_T)=closure(π Z_T): inclusion one way follows from continuity, and the other from taking a convergent subsequence in the bounded closure. The missing set between a semialgebraic set and its closure has dimension less than the target dimension, so its target-dimensional volume is zero. Sum over π_I; monotonicity treats B_T.
acceptance: Open and closed boxes have the same volume and projection volumes although their lattice-point counts can differ.
A planar line segment has zero planar volume; its frontier is the whole segment.
Boundedness is necessary for π closure=closure π: the hyperbola xy=1 has a nonclosed coordinate projection.

sources.match: Provides precisely the closure/frontier and projection-volume equalities used to remove compactness in Theorem 1.3.
The closure-minus-set dimension drop is consumed from the owner.

nodes.title: Uniform comparison of orthogonal and coordinate projections
nodes.statement: For a fixed semialgebraic family Z⊆ℝ^{m+n} with bounded fibres and 1≤j≤n, there is c_{Z,j} such that the j-volume of every orthogonal projection of Z_T to any j-plane is at most c_{Z,j} V_j(Z_T), uniformly in T and the plane. The same holds for closure Z_T.
proofSteps: Parametrize the projection plane by φ∈O(n); let p:ℝⁿ→ℝ^j take the first j coordinates. The family of images pφ(closure Z_T) is semialgebraic. Apply the owner’s semialgebraic choice to the graph of (φ,T,x)↦pφx to select a semialgebraic section over each image. Its image S_{φ,T} lies in closure Z_T, has dimension at most j by injectivity of pφ on it, and has the same orthogonal projection as closure Z_T. No continuity of the selection is required.
Orthogonal projection is 1-Lipschitz; hence its j-volume is at most H^j(S_{φ,T}). Apply semialgebraic-hausdorff-bound to this single family of sections, obtaining a constant independent of φ,T.

Every coordinate projection of S_{φ,T} lies in the corresponding projection of closure Z_T. Bound their volumes by V_j(closure Z_T)=V_j(Z_T), using semialgebraic-boundary-null. This is the missing Proposition 6.1 step after the linear-algebraic projection estimate.
acceptance: For a diagonal line segment the largest one-dimensional projection is at most the sum of its coordinate lengths.
For j=n the comparison is equality of volume.
Arbitrary sets need not admit a family-uniform bound; the semialgebraic family, not just each individual fibre, is fixed.

sources.locator: Proposition 6.1, pp.17,20; Lemma 6.2 and proof, pp.17–20
sources.match: The family of definable sections supplies a j-dimensional subset with unchanged chosen orthogonal projection; Lemma 5.8 controls its measure by coordinate projections.

nodes.title: Lattice points in semialgebraic families, uniformly in the lattice
nodes.statement: Let m, n ≥ 1 and Z ⊆ ℝ^{m+n} semialgebraic with bounded fibres Z_T = {x : (T, x) ∈ Z}, T ∈ ℝ^m. There is c_Z depending only on Z such that for every full lattice Λ ⊆ ℝⁿ with successive minima λ_1 ≤ … ≤ λ_n and every T: |#(Z_T ∩ Λ) − vol(Z_T)/det Λ| ≤ c_Z·Σ_{j=0}^{n−1} V_j(Z_T)/(λ_1⋯λ_j), with V_j the coordinate projection volumes (V_0 = 1).
hypotheses: Only semialgebraic families are claimed here; the source proves the statement for families definable in any o-minimal structure, which no library or roadmap plans.
proofSteps: For compact fibres C_T, choose an adapted lattice basis and send it to the standard basis by Ψ. The family (Ψ,T)↦Ψ(C_T) has a uniform Davenport line-section constant by semialgebraic-interval-condition. Its main volume is vol C_T/detΛ.

BW Lemma 2.2 expresses each j-dimensional transformed coordinate projection using oblique projections onto spans of j basis vectors, with factor at most 2^j/(V_j^{ball} λ₁⋯λ_j). Lemmas 2.3–2.4 use the adapted basis lengths and Minkowski’s second theorem to bound the angle distortion of these oblique projections by a dimension constant times the largest j-dimensional orthogonal projection. Equivalently, the complementary basis parallelepiped has volume ≪_n λ_{j+1}⋯λ_n and detΛ≳_n∏λ_i, which bounds the inverse angle factor. These are linear-algebra steps and do not yet compare coordinate and arbitrary orthogonal projections.

Apply orthogonal-projection-comparison to C_T. It turns the arbitrary orthogonal projection bound into c_Z V_j(Z_T)/(λ₁⋯λ_j), with c_Z independent of Λ and T. Sum Davenport’s finitely many projection terms; the j=0 contribution is one.

For arbitrary bounded Z_T apply the compact-fibre result twice, to C_T and B_T=frontier Z_T. By semialgebraic-boundary-null, vol B_T=0, vol C_T=vol Z_T and V_j(B_T)≤V_j(C_T)=V_j(Z_T). Since C_T\Z_T⊆B_T, the difference of the lattice counts is at most #(B_T∩Λ). Adding the two errors proves the displayed estimate without any assumption on which boundary points are included.
acceptance: Λ = ℤⁿ and Z_T = T·[0,1]ⁿ (T ∈ ℝ_{>0}): recovers |(⌊T⌋ + 1)ⁿ − Tⁿ| ≪ Σ_j T^j.
The example of Barroero–Widmer p.5 (union of axis segments of length T shifted by λ_j e_j) shows the j-th term cannot be dropped.

sources.locator: Theorem 1.3, p.5; Lemmas 2.1–2.4, pp.7–8; Lemma 5.8, pp.15–17; Proposition 6.1 and Lemma 6.2, pp.17–20; §7, pp.20–21 (arXiv:1210.5943, retrieved 2026-10-16)
sources.match: For a definable family with bounded fibres, |#(Z_T ∩ Λ) − vol(Z_T)/det Λ| ≤ c_Z Σ_{j<n} V_j(Z_T)/(λ_1⋯λ_j); semialgebraic families are definable.
Uses Theorem 1.3 of Barroero–Widmer for the semialgebraic regions R_v(T, γ).

nodes.title: Angular bands and their lattice regions
nodes.statement: Let N ≥ 1, γ > 0 and v ∈ ℝ^N. The angular band of v is C_v^{(γ)} = {t ∈ ℝ^N : |⟨v, t⟩| ≤ ‖v‖·‖t‖/(2γ)}, the set of vectors making an angle with the hyperplane v^⊥ whose sine is at most 1/(2γ). For v_1, …, v_I ∈ ℝ^N and T > 0 put R_v(T, γ) = B̄_N(T) ∩ C_{v_1}^{(γ)} ∩ ⋯ ∩ C_{v_I}^{(γ)}, and for a lattice Λ of rank R put V_v(Λ; γ) = vol_R(span_ℝ Λ ∩ R_v(1, γ)), the R-dimensional volume in the span.
hypotheses: γ > 0; v = 0 gives the whole space (the inequality reads 0 ≤ 0).
The band is a closed cone (invariant under t ↦ ct for c ∈ ℝ), so R_v(T, γ) = T·R_v(1, γ).
proofSteps: The band is defined by the polynomial inequality 4γ²⟨v,t⟩² ≤ ‖v‖²‖t‖², so R_v(T, γ) has complexity (I + 1, 2) (semialgebraic-complexity).
Homogeneity: C_v^{(γ)} is closed under real scalar multiplication, hence R_v(T, γ) = T·R_v(1, γ) and V_v depends on Λ only through span_ℝ Λ.
acceptance: For N = 2, v = e_1 and γ = 1/2 the band is all of ℝ² (|t_1| ≤ ‖t‖ always).
For N = 2, v = e_1, γ = 1 the band is {|t_1| ≤ ‖t‖/2}, two sectors of half-angle π/6 around the t_2-axis.

nodes.title: Lattice points in intersections of angular bands
nodes.statement: Let N ≥ 2, 1 ≤ R ≤ N, 1 ≤ I ≤ N − 1, Λ ⊆ ℝ^N a lattice of rank R, v_1, …, v_I ∈ ℝ^N and γ > 0. Let Y ≥ λ_R(Λ). For T ≥ Y: #(Λ ∩ R_v(T, γ)) = (T^R/det Λ)·(V_v(Λ; γ) + O(Y/T)), the implied constant depending only on N and I (and on R).
hypotheses: The constant is uniform in Λ, the v_i and γ.
The source states dependence on R only; the uniformity in the family follows from the semialgebraic family bound, whose constant depends on the family (N, I): recorded as a dependence on (N, I).
proofSteps: Rotate span_ℝ Λ onto ℝ^R × {0} by an orthogonal map; the region becomes a semialgebraic family in the parameters (v, γ, T) of complexity depending only on (N, I).
Apply semialgebraic-family-lattice-count: the error is ≪ Σ_{i=1}^{R} T^{R−i}/(λ_1⋯λ_{R−i}).
By Minkowski's second theorem λ_1⋯λ_{R−i} ≍ det Λ/(λ_{R−i+1}⋯λ_R) ≥ det Λ/Y^i, so each error term is ≪ (T^R/det Λ)(Y/T)^i ≤ (T^R/det Λ)(Y/T) for T ≥ Y.
acceptance: I = 1, v_1 = 0: the region is the ball, V_v = V_R and the formula is the classical ball count with error T^{R−1}Y/det Λ.

sources.match: States the asymptotic count with error O(Y/T) for T ≥ Y ≥ λ_R(Λ), using Barroero–Widmer Theorem 1.3 and Minkowski's second theorem.
The uniform family count.

nodes.title: Primitive integral lattices with prescribed dyadic minima
nodes.statement: Let n ≥ 2, 1 ≤ r ≤ n + 1 and s_1, …, s_r ≥ 1. S_{r,n}(s_1, …, s_r) is the set of primitive lattices L ⊆ ℤ^{n+1} of rank r (L = span_ℝ L ∩ ℤ^{n+1}) whose Euclidean successive minima satisfy s_j/2 < λ_j(L) ≤ s_j for every j.
hypotheses: Primitive means saturated in ℤ^{n+1}; the minima are computed in span_ℝ L.
proofSteps: A rank-r primitive lattice is determined by its real span, so S_{r,n} is a set of rational subspaces of dimension r.
Finiteness: λ_r(L) ≤ s_r bounds a basis of L, so only finitely many L occur (ball-count-successive-minima).
acceptance: S_{1,n}(s) is the set of lines ℤx with x primitive and s/2 < ‖x‖ ≤ s.
For r = n + 1 the only primitive lattice is ℤ^{n+1}, with all minima 1: it lies in S_{n+1,n}(s) iff 1 ≤ s_j < 2 for all j.

nodes.title: Primitive extensions of a fixed primitive lattice
nodes.statement: Let n ≥ 2, 2 ≤ r ≤ n + 1 and L' ⊆ ℤ^{n+1} a primitive lattice of rank r − 1. For s ≥ 1, the number of primitive lattices L ⊆ ℤ^{n+1} of rank r with L' ⊆ L and det(L)/det(L') ≤ s is ≪_n s^{n−r+2}·det(L').
hypotheses: The implied constant depends only on n.
proofSteps: L ↦ π(L) with π the orthogonal projection away from span L' identifies such L with primitive vectors of the rank-(n − r + 2) quotient lattice π(ℤ^{n+1}) of norm ≤ s, up to sign (det L = det L'·‖π(x)‖).

M = π(ℤ^{n+1}) has rank q = n − r + 2, determinant 1/det(L') (GN.0 covolume-projection) and integral dual M* = L'^⊥ (GN.0 dual-projection-comap). Integrality gives λ_i(M*) ≥ 1, so transference-minkowski-constant bounds every minimum μ_i of M by a constant c(q).
By ball-count-successive-minima the number of x ∈ M with ‖x‖ ≤ s is ≪ Σ_j s^j/(μ_1⋯μ_j) = Σ_j s^j μ_{j+1}⋯μ_q/(μ_1⋯μ_q) ≪ s^q·det(L') for s ≥ 1, using μ_1⋯μ_q ≍ det M (Minkowski's second theorem).
acceptance: r = 2, L' = ℤe_1: the extensions correspond to primitive x ∈ ℤ^n (the other coordinates) with ‖x‖ ≤ s, about s^n of them.

sources.locator: Proof of Lemma 3.18, p.19, citing Schmidt, Duke Math. J. 35 (1968), Lemma 6 with i = 1

nodes.title: Counting primitive lattices by their minima
hypotheses: The implied constant depends only on n.
proofSteps: For L∈S_{r,n}, choose independent minima vectors b_1,…,b_{r−1} and let M=(spanℝ{b_i})∩ℤ^{n+1}. Since L is saturated, M⊆L, while M contains b_1,…,b_{r−1}. Thus λ_j(M)=λ_j(L) for j<r, not merely an upper bound: M lies in S_{r−1,n}(s_1,…,s_{r−1}). Its covolume is ≪s_1⋯s_{r−1} by Minkowski. The induction hypothesis counts M directly; no additional dyadic decomposition is needed.
Given L^{(−1)}, det(L)/det(L^{(−1)}) ≪ s_r, so schmidt-primitive-extension-count bounds the number of L by s_r^{n−r+2}·det(L^{(−1)}); multiply.
acceptance: r = 1: the bound s_1^{n+1} is the order of the number of primitive vectors of norm ≤ s_1.
r = n + 1: the bound is ∏ s_j^{2n+3−2j} ≥ 1, while the true count is ≤ 1.

sources.match: States #S_{r,n}(s_1, …, s_r) ≪ s_1^{n+r}s_2^{n+r−2}⋯s_r^{n−r+2} and proves it by induction on r.

nodes.title: One-band and two-band section volumes
nodes.statement: For N ≥ 2 and w, z ∈ ℝ^N let I(w, z) = vol_{N−1}{t ∈ (ℝw)^⊥ : |⟨z, t⟩| ≤ ‖t‖ ≤ 1} (volume in the hyperplane w^⊥, w ≠ 0) and J(w, z) = vol_N{t ∈ ℝ^N : |⟨w, t⟩| ≤ ‖t‖, |⟨z, t⟩| ≤ ‖t‖, ‖t‖ ≤ 1}. Put δ(w, z) = ‖w‖²‖z‖² − ⟨w, z⟩², which is > 0 exactly when w, z are linearly independent.
hypotheses: w ≠ 0 for I; no condition for J (J = V_N when ‖w‖, ‖z‖ ≤ 1).
proofSteps: Both sets are compact semialgebraic, so the volumes are finite; I is a volume in a hyperplane, computed via an isometry w^⊥ ≃ ℝ^{N−1}.
Invariance: I(Ow, Oz) = I(w, z) and J(Ow, Oz) = J(w, z) for orthogonal O; I(cw, z) = I(w, z) for c ≠ 0.
acceptance: If ‖z‖ ≤ 1 then I(w, z) = V_{N−1}.
δ(w, z) = 0 for dependent vectors.

nodes.title: Asymptotics of the band section volumes
nodes.statement: Let N ≥ 3 and w, z ∈ ℝ^N linearly independent, δ = δ(w, z). Then I(w, z) = (2(N − 2)/(N − 1))·V_{N−2}·‖w‖/δ^{1/2}·(1 + O_N(min{1, ‖w‖²/δ})), and J(w, z) = (4(N − 2)/N)·V_{N−2}/δ^{1/2}·(1 + O_N(min{1, (‖w‖ + ‖z‖)²/δ})).
hypotheses: N ≥ 3; the asymptotics are informative when δ is large compared with ‖w‖² (resp. (‖w‖+‖z‖)²).
proofSteps: Put z′=z−⟨z,w⟩w/‖w‖² and R=‖z′‖=√δ/‖w‖. When R≤1 the band in w⊥ is the whole unit ball and the displayed relative O(1) is valid. When R>1, choose the first coordinate along z′; solving R²u²≤u²+‖v‖² gives |u|≤‖v‖/√(R²−1). For R bounded use the whole-ball bound, and for R≥√2 replace √(R²−1) by R with relative O(R⁻²). Fubini then gives (2/R)∫_{B^{N−2}}‖v‖dv, with the same relative error after truncation by the unit ball. The radial moment is (N−2)V_{N−2}/(N−1).

For J, take coordinates u_1=⟨w,t⟩, u_2=⟨z,t⟩ and v∈{w,z}⊥. The Jacobian is δ⁻¹/² and ‖t‖²=q(u_1,u_2)+‖v‖², where q=‖u_1z−u_2w‖²/δ. The region is max(u_1²,u_2²)≤q+‖v‖²≤1. If η=(‖w‖+‖z‖)²/δ≥1 its volume is O_N(δ⁻¹/²), since |u_i|≤1 and ‖v‖≤1.

If η<1, then q≤η on |u_i|≤1. Sandwich the region by replacing q with 0 and shifting the radial inequalities by η. Integration over u_1,u_2 gives 4∫_{B^{N−2}}‖v‖²dv·(1+O_N(η)); the moment is (N−2)V_{N−2}/N. These two computations give exactly the constants in the statement.
acceptance: When w ⊥ z with ‖w‖ = 1 and ‖z‖ = R large, I ≈ 2(N − 2)V_{N−2}/((N − 1)R).

proofSteps: S_k(Λ; R) = Σ_{m ≥ 1} m^{−k} S*_k(Λ ∩ ..., R/m)-type decompositions hold only for primitive Λ (a ∈ Λ primitive in ℤ^N iff primitive in Λ when Λ is primitive).
S*_0(Λ; B̄(T)) counts primitive points; S_0 counts all nonzero points.

nodes.title: Primitive points of a primitive lattice in a ball
nodes.statement: Let N ≥ 3, 3 ≤ R ≤ N, Λ ⊆ ℤ^N a primitive lattice of rank R and Y ≥ 1 such that B̄_N(Y) contains R linearly independent vectors of Λ (λ_R(Λ) ≤ Y). For T ≥ Y: S*_0(Λ; B̄_N(T)) = V_R T^R/(ζ(R) det Λ)·(1 + O_R(Y/T)) + O_R(T log(2Y)).
hypotheses: Primitive Λ, so primitivity in Λ and in ℤ^N agree; R ≥ 3 makes the Möbius sum converge with a log error.
proofSteps: Because Λ is saturated in ℤ^N, the ambient content of a nonzero vector divides it inside Λ. Möbius inversion therefore gives Σ_{m≤T} μ(m)(N_Λ(T/m)−1); integral nonzero vectors have Euclidean norm at least one, explaining the finite cutoff.

For m≤T/Y, use the rank-R ball estimate N_Λ(t)=V_R t^R/detΛ·(1+O_R(Y/t)), valid for t≥Y. The main Möbius series has tail O_R((Y/T)^{R−1}); since R≥3, Σm^{1−R} is bounded. Both errors are O_R(Y T^{R−1}/detΛ). The removal of zero contributes O(T).
For T/Y<m≤T use small-vector-count with R₀=R−2: N_Λ(T/m) ≪_R T²Y^{R−2}/(m²detΛ)+T/m. Summing m⁻² over the tail gives O_R(TY^{R−1}/detΛ), bounded by O_R(YT^{R−1}/detΛ) because Y≤T and R≥3.

The harmonic tail Σ_{T/Y<m≤T}T/m is O(T(1+log Y)). Combine this with the O(T) zero-vector term to obtain O_R(T log(2Y)), including Y=1. Le Boudec writes log Y, with the O(T) term absorbed elsewhere; log(2Y) makes the displayed independent additive error valid at the endpoint.
acceptance: Λ = ℤ^3, Y = 1: the number of primitive vectors of norm ≤ T is (4π/3)T³/ζ(3) + O(T²) ⊂ the stated form.

sources.match: Lemma 3 is the direct parameter-uniform statement for saturated rank-R integral lattices, R≥3, λ_R≤Y≤T. Its proof supplies the short-radius tail estimate and constants depending only on R.

nodes.title: Symmetric matrices with prescribed row space
nodes.statement: Let n ≥ 2 and S = Sym²(n) the real symmetric n×n matrices with the Frobenius Euclidean norm (identify S with ℝ^{n(n+1)/2} so that off-diagonal coordinates carry weight √2; covolumes are taken for this norm). For a lattice Λ ⊆ ℤⁿ of rank r, S(Λ) is the set of B ∈ S(ℤ) whose row space is contained in Λ ⊗ ℝ, and S'(Λ) the lattice it spans; the full-rank part S(Λ)^{full} consists of those B whose row space is all of Λ ⊗ ℝ. For v, w ∈ ℝⁿ put v ∗ w = vwᵀ + wvᵀ if v, w are linearly independent and v ∗ w = vwᵀ otherwise. For s = diag(t_1^{−1}, …, t_n^{−1}) with t_i > 0 and 1 ≤ r < n put C(r, s) = ∏_{1≤i<j≤n, j>n−r} t_i/t_j. SL_n(ℝ) acts on S by γ·A = γAγᵀ.
hypotheses: The full-rank subset and the spanning lattice are different objects (PAPER-BHARGAVA-SHANKAR-WANG-25/E18); counts of rank-r matrices fibre over the saturated row lattice.
C(r, s) is a product over the pairs (i, j) with i < j and j > n − r.
Throughout the skew-counting chain s=diag(t_1⁻¹,…,t_n⁻¹), t_i>0 and ∏t_i=1. Fix κ>0 and use the Siegel cone t_i≥κt_{i+1}; its implied constants may depend on n and κ.
proofSteps: v ∗ w is symmetric with row space in span{v, w} and ‖v‖‖w‖ ≤ ‖v ∗ w‖ ≤ 2‖v‖‖w‖ in the Frobenius norm.
Every rank-r integral symmetric matrix has a unique saturated row lattice Λ = rowspace ∩ ℤⁿ, primitive of rank r, and lies in S(Λ)^{full}.
γ(S(Λ)) = {γBγᵀ : B ∈ S(Λ)} has row spaces in γΛ ⊗ ℝ.

nodes.title: A reduced basis for the symmetric row lattice
nodes.statement: Let γ ∈ SL_n(ℝ), Λ ⊆ ℤⁿ primitive of rank r and ℓ_1, …, ℓ_r a basis of γΛ. Then {ℓ_i ∗ ℓ_j : 1 ≤ i ≤ j ≤ r} is a basis of γ(S'(Λ)), and the covolume of γ(S'(Λ)) in its span is 2^{r(r−1)/4}·d(γΛ)^{r+1}, where d(γΛ) is the covolume of γΛ in its span. If {ℓ_i} is almost reduced (∏‖ℓ_i‖ ≪_n d(γΛ)), so is {ℓ_i ∗ ℓ_j}.
hypotheses: d(γΛ) ≠ d(Λ) in general: an element of SL_n(ℝ) preserves n-dimensional covolume only (PAPER-BHARGAVA-SHANKAR-WANG-25/E15).
Almost reduced bases exist (adapted-basis-coordinates).
proofSteps: Choose a ℤ-basis e_1, …, e_r of Λ; S'(Λ) is the image of Sym²(ℤ^r) under X ↦ EXEᵀ, E the n×r matrix of the basis, with basis {e_i ∗ e_j}.
Apply γ: γ(e_i ∗ e_j)γᵀ = γe_i ∗ γe_j, and change basis within γΛ.

Covolume: the map Sym²(ℝ^r) → S, X ↦ FXFᵀ (F the matrix of ℓ) scales Frobenius covolume by det(FᵀF)^{(r+1)/2} = d(γΛ)^{r+1}; the factor 2^{r(r−1)/4} comes from the √2 weights of the off-diagonal coordinates against the basis vectors ℓ_i ∗ ℓ_j.
acceptance: r = 1, Λ = ℤv: S'(Λ) = ℤ·vvᵀ, covolume ‖vvᵀ‖ = ‖v‖² = d(Λ)², matching 2^0 d^2.

nodes.title: Minima conditions for a nonempty count
nodes.statement: Let γ ∈ SL_n(ℝ), Λ ⊆ ℤⁿ primitive of rank r with γΛ having successive minima μ_1 ≤ … ≤ μ_r, D ⊆ S(ℝ) bounded and Y > 0. If Y·D ∩ γ(S(Λ)^{full}) ≠ ∅ then μ_iμ_j ≤ c_1Y for all i, j with i + j ≤ r + 1, with c_1 depending on n and D.
hypotheses: The nonempty intersection is with the full-rank part: a matrix whose row space is all of γΛ ⊗ ℝ (E18).
proofSteps: Write a full-rank B ∈ YD ∩ γ(S(Λ)) as Σ_{k≤l} b_kl ℓ_k ∗ ℓ_l in an almost reduced basis ℓ of γΛ. If μ_iμ_j > c_1Y for some i + j ≤ r + 1, every basis vector ℓ_k ∗ ℓ_l with k ≥ i, l ≥ j has length ≥ μ_kμ_l > c_1Y, so its coefficient vanishes (almost-reducedness bounds |b_kl| by ‖B‖/‖ℓ_k ∗ ℓ_l‖ up to a constant).
Then the Gram matrix of B in the basis ℓ has a zero block in rows i..r and columns j..r, of total size (r − i + 1) + (r − j + 1) ≥ r + 1 > r, so B has rank < r, a contradiction.
The pigeonhole on the anti-diagonal i + j = r + 1 is Eskin–Katznelson's Lemma 4.1.
acceptance: r = 1: the condition is μ_1² ≤ c_1Y, i.e. the generator of γΛ has ‖v‖² ≪ Y.

sources.locator: Proposition 5.4, p.24 (author copy dated 4 April 2025); arXiv v1 p.22
sources.match: If the count is positive then µ_iµ_j ≤ c_1Y for i + j ≤ r + 1.

nodes.title: Counting symmetric matrices with a fixed row lattice
nodes.statement: Let γ ∈ SL_n(ℝ), Λ ⊆ ℤⁿ primitive of rank r with γΛ having minima μ_1 ≤ … ≤ μ_r, D ⊆ S(ℝ) bounded and Y ≥ 1. Then #(Y·D ∩ γ(S(Λ)^{full})) ≪_{n,D} (Y^{r(r+1)/2}/d(γΛ)^{r+1})·∏_{1≤i<j≤r, i+j≤r+1} μ_j/μ_i.
hypotheses: The denominator is d(γΛ)^{r+1}, not d(Λ)^{r+1} (E15).
Counting is over the full-rank part; the spanning lattice S'(Λ) is used only for the lattice-point bound.
proofSteps: Put m=r(r+1)/2 and choose an almost reduced basis of γΛ with lengths ≍_nμ_i. Its symmetric products form an almost reduced basis of γ(S′(Λ)), of lengths ≍_nμ_iμ_j and covolume ≍_n d(γΛ)^{r+1}. The bounded-domain lattice count therefore gives ∏_{i≤j}max(1,CY/(μ_iμ_j)), with C depending on n,D. Equivalently this is ≪Y^m/d(γΛ)^{r+1} times ∏_{(i,j)∈U_Y}μ_iμ_j/(CY), where U_Y={i≤j:μ_iμ_j>CY}. The product includes only lengths above the counting scale, not the entire upper antidiagonal.

If the full-rank count is zero the conclusion is immediate. Otherwise nonvanishing gives μ_{r+1−j}μ_j≤C₀Y. Choose C≥C₀, so U_Y⊆{i≤j:i+j>r+1}. For a pair in U_Y, μ_iμ_j/(CY)≤(C₀/C)μ_i/μ_{r+1−j}. The injection (i,j)↦(r+1−j,i) lands in {k<l:k+l≤r+1}. Each omitted ratio μ_l/μ_k is at least one, so the restricted product is bounded by the full product in the statement. The finite number of dimension-dependent constants is harmless.
acceptance: r = 1: the bound is Y/d(γΛ)² = Y/μ_1², the count of b with |b|μ_1² ≪ Y.

For r=2, γ=1 and Λ=ℤe_1+ℤe_2⊂ℤ³ all μ_i=1. There are ≍Y³ full-rank 2×2 symmetric blocks. Multiplying by 1/Y from the whole upper antidiagonal would falsely give O(Y²); U_Y is empty for large Y and the corrected intermediate bound is O(Y³).

sources.locator: Proposition 5.5 and proof, (26)–(28), p.24 (author copy dated 4 April 2025); arXiv v1 (24)–(26), p.22
sources.match: The source denominator must be d(γΛ)^{r+1} (the previously reviewed E15). The proof also wrongly identifies the whole upper antidiagonal with minima above Y. E403 records this separate proof error; restricting the product to U_Y repairs it without changing the final ratio bound.

nodes.title: Counting row lattices with prescribed skew minima
nodes.statement: Fix n≥2, 1≤r<n and κ>0. Let s=diag(t_1⁻¹,…,t_n⁻¹), with t_i>0, ∏t_i=1 and t_i≥κt_{i+1}. For 0<L_1≤⋯≤L_r, let Σ(L,s) consist of primitive rank-r Λ⊆ℤⁿ whose minima μ_i of s⁻¹Λ satisfy L_i≤μ_i<2L_i. (a) If Σ(L,s) is nonempty, then L_i/t_j≥c(n,κ)>0 whenever i+j≥n+1. (b) #Σ(L,s)≪_{n,κ}(L_1⋯L_r)^n ∏_{i<j≤r}(L_i/L_j) C(r,s).
hypotheses: The cone parameter κ is fixed. All lower-bound and counting constants may depend on it; no uniformity over varying Siegel cones is claimed.
proofSteps: (a) Choose independent vectors ℓ_i∈Λ realizing the successive minima of s⁻¹Λ, so |s⁻¹ℓ_i|<2L_i; they need not be an integral basis. Their integer coordinates satisfy |ℓ_{ij}|≤2L_i/t_j. If L_k/t_{n+1−k} is sufficiently small in terms of n,κ, all entries with i≤k,j≤n+1−k vanish. Then the first k independent vectors lie in a (k−1)-dimensional coordinate space, a contradiction. The cone inequalities extend the conclusion to every i+j≥n+1.

(b) Use adapted-basis-coordinates to choose an actual basis b_i of s⁻¹Λ with |b_i|≤A_nL_i. For every i<j choose independent integers m_{ij} with |m_{ij}|≤L_j/L_i and replace b_j by b_j+Σ_{i<j}m_{ij}b_i. These are distinct bases of the same lattice, each with j-th length ≤A′_nL_j. Thus each Λ contributes ≫_n∏_{i<j}L_j/L_i tuples to this enlarged bounded box. Count all integer coordinate tuples in that box and divide by this multiplicity. Exact dyadic bounds on the lengths of a reduced integral basis are not assumed.

For each i, the coordinate-box count is ≪_{n,κ}L_i^n∏_{j≤α(i)}(t_j/L_i), where α(i) is the last coordinate for which L_i/t_j is below a fixed small threshold (the cone absorbs bounded ordering changes). Part (a) gives α(i)≤n−i. The first omitted coordinate has L_i/t_{α(i)+1} bounded below; insert this factor for each preceding j to bound ∏_{j≤α(i)}t_j/L_i by a constant times ∏_{j≤n−i}t_j/t_{n−i+1}. Multiply over i to get C(r,s), and combine with the basis multiplicity factor.
acceptance: s = 1 (all t_i = 1): (b) reads #Σ ≪ (L_1⋯L_r)^n∏(L_i/L_j), the count of primitive rank-r lattices with minima ≍ L_i (compare primitive-lattice-minima-count).

Independent minima vectors suffice for the vanishing-coordinate contradiction. The count of lattices instead uses actual bases with dimension-dependent length bounds and divides by their triangular shear multiplicity ∏L_j/L_i.

nodes.title: Singular integral symmetric matrices in skewed balls
nodes.statement: Fix n≥2, 1≤r<n, Θ>0, κ>0 and endpoint constants C₀,c₀>0. Let D⊆Sym²(n)(ℝ) be bounded, Y≥2 and s=diag(t_1⁻¹,…,t_n⁻¹), with t_i>0, ∏t_i=1, t_i≥κt_{i+1}, t_1≤C₀Y^Θ and t_n≥c₀Y⁻Θ. For integral symmetric matrices of rank exactly r, N_r(Y,s)=#(s(YD)∩S(ℤ)^{(r)}) satisfies N_r(Y,s)≪_{n,Θ,κ,D,C₀,c₀}C(r,s)Y^{nr/2}(log Y)^r.
hypotheses: The cone and endpoint constants are fixed, and the implied constant depends on them. The skew notation always uses inverse diagonal entries.
proofSteps: Fibre the rank-r matrices by their saturated row lattice Λ (symmetric-row-lattices): N_r(Y, s) = Σ_Λ #(Y·D ∩ s^{−1}(S(Λ)^{full})) after transporting by γ = s^{−1}.
Decompose the Λ dyadically by the minima of s^{−1}Λ (sets Σ(L, s)); eskin-katznelson-nonvanishing and skew-row-lattice-count (a) confine L to O((log Y)^r) dyadic boxes.

In each dyadic box combine row-lattice-matrix-count, d(s⁻¹Λ)≍_nL_1⋯L_r and skew-row-lattice-count. The two ratio products cancel on i+j≤r+1; all remaining L_i/L_j≤1. The product bound L_1⋯L_r≪Y^{r/2}, raised to n−r−1≥0, leaves C(r,s)Y^{nr/2}. Sum over O_{n,Θ,κ,D,C₀,c₀}((log Y)^r) boxes.
acceptance: s = 1: N_r(Y, 1) ≪ Y^{nr/2}(log Y)^r, the Eskin–Katznelson upper bound for rank-r symmetric matrices of norm ≤ Y.
The restriction Y ≥ 2 avoids a vanishing (log Y)^r as Y decreases to 1 while a fixed nonzero integral singular matrix can remain in the region.

sources.locator: Theorem 5.1, p.23 and proof, p.26 (author copy dated 4 April 2025); arXiv v1 pp.20,23–24
sources.match: States N_r(Y, s) = O(C(r, s)Y^{nr/2} log^r Y) uniformly for s ∈ T′ with t_1 ≪ Y^Θ, t_n ≫ Y^{−Θ}; proved by summing Proposition 5.5 over dyadic ranges using Proposition 5.7.

nodes.title: Planar domains with a curvature-controlled lattice count
nodes.statement: A C² convex planar domain is a compact convex E ⊆ ℝ² with nonempty interior whose boundary is a C² curve of nowhere vanishing curvature; A(E) is its area and R_max(E) the maximum radius of curvature of ∂E. For C > 0 and θ > 0, L(C, θ) is the class of C² convex planar domains E such that for every integer a ≥ 1 and every x₀ ∈ ℤ² with A(E) ≥ a²: |#(a^{−1}(E − x₀) ∩ ℤ²) − a^{−2}A(E)| ≤ C·(R_max(E)/a)^θ. An exponent θ is admissible (for integral binary forms) if some C makes every ellipse {Q ≤ X}, Q a positive definite integral binary quadratic form and X > 0, belong to L(C, θ).
hypotheses: The estimate is uniform over integer translates x₀ and integer scalings a, as the sieve applications require.
Ellipses of definite integral binary forms have analytic boundary of nonzero curvature.
proofSteps: Membership is a uniform family of lattice counts for the dilates a^{−1}(E − x₀), equivalently counts of the lattice aℤ² + x₀ in E.
For θ′ ≥ θ, A(E) ≤ πR_max(E)² gives R_max(E)/a ≥ π^{−1/2}. Thus L(C,θ) ⊆ L(C·π^{(θ′−θ)/2},θ′). One may then increase C further; the constant cannot in general be left unchanged.
acceptance: Every disc of radius ρ has R_max = ρ and lies in L(C, 2/3) for an absolute C (van der Corput).
A square is not C² convex in this sense (curvature vanishes on its sides), so it is not in any L(C, θ).

sources.locator: §9, the class L(C_l, θ_l) before Remark 9.5, p.69, and Definition 10.8, p.90 (arXiv:1710.04557v3)
sources.match: Defines L(C_l, θ_l) by the uniform count over integer translates and scalings and calls θ_l admissible when all ellipses of definite integral binary forms lie in L(C_l, θ_l).
Fixes the curvature conventions (class C^k boundaries, r_min, r_max) for plane convex domains.

nodes.title: Fourier decay of an ellipse with its full shape dependence
nodes.statement: There is an absolute C such that for every planar ellipse E=c+T(B̄₂), with singular values A≥B>0, and every ξ≠0, |∫_E exp(−2πi⟨ξ,x⟩)dx|≤C AB(1+|Tᵀξ|)^{−3/2}≤C√R |ξ|^{−3/2}, where R=A²/B is its maximal radius of curvature. Constants are independent of A/B and c.
proofSteps: A linear change of variables and a rotation take the transform to AB times the unit-disc transform at s=|Tᵀξ|; translation only supplies a unit-modulus phase. Integrating cross sections gives the one-dimensional integral ∫_{−1}^1 2√(1−v²) exp(−2πisv)dv. This is also the explicit integral underlying KN (3.19)–(3.20).

For s≤2 use the disc area. For s>2 remove endpoint intervals of length δ=1/s, whose integrals are O(δ^{3/2}). On [−1+δ,1−δ] integrate twice by parts. Endpoint values of √(1−v²) are O(√δ), endpoint first derivatives are O(δ^{-1/2}), and the integral of the absolute second derivative is O(δ^{-1/2}). Every resulting term is O(s^{-3/2}). Thus a finite absolute constant follows without depending on the numerical Bessel maximum or an unread special-function reference.
Finally |Tᵀξ|≥B|ξ|, so AB(1+|Tᵀξ|)^{-3/2}≤(A/√B)|ξ|^{-3/2}=√R |ξ|^{-3/2}. This is the precise quantitative primary-source Fourier contract used in the uniform ellipse count.
acceptance: A=B=a gives the familiar a^{1/2}|ξ|^{-3/2} disc bound.
For ξ in the short-axis direction, the coefficient A/√B grows with eccentricity; a shape-independent area-normalized coefficient would be false.
Translating the ellipse changes only the Fourier phase, hence leaves the estimate unchanged.

sources.match: Gives the ellipse-transform integral and its support-function dependence. The elementary endpoint proof here replaces the numerical Bessel bound and retains all shape dependence.

nodes.title: Uniform van der Corput exponent for every ellipse
nodes.statement: There is an absolute C such that for every real planar ellipse E, in every orientation and with arbitrary centre, |#(E∩ℤ²)−area(E)|≤C(1+R_max(E))^{2/3}. No lower bound on the smaller semiaxis and no bounded-eccentricity hypothesis is imposed.
proofSteps: Write the semiaxes A≥B>0 and R=A²/B. If R<1 then A≤R<1, so the ellipse meets at most nine integer points and has bounded area. Assume R≥1 and put δ=(1/4)R^{-1/3}.

If B<2δ, then A=√(RB)≤√(2Rδ)≪R^{1/3}. Davenport’s compact convex estimate in dimension two gives error O(1+V₁(E))=O(1+A), enough for the asserted bound. This explicitly handles arbitrarily thin ellipses and avoids an invalid inner smoothing.

If B≥2δ, put r=δ/B≤1/2 and let E_± be the concentric ellipses with axes (1±r)A,(1±r)B. Choose one fixed nonnegative C∞ bump of mass one supported in the unit disc and rescale it to radius δ. Since the centred ellipse contains the B-disc, E_-+δB̄₂⊆E and E+δB̄₂⊆E_+. Thus 1_{E_-}*η_δ≤1_E≤1_{E_+}*η_δ pointwise, including lattice points on the boundary. The two main integrals differ from area(E) by O(Aδ)≤O(Rδ).

Apply Poisson to each smooth compactly supported convolution. The required ℤ² identity is obtained by applying pinned SchwartzMap.tsum_eq_tsum_fourier successively to both coordinates; Schwartz estimates justify all sum/integral interchanges. The nonzero Fourier coefficients are bounded by ellipse-fourier-decay and |η̂_δ(m)|≤C_N(1+δ|m|)^{-N}, obtained by integration by parts for this fixed bump. R_max(E_±)≤(3/2)R.

Summing over dyadic Euclidean annuli, which contain O(2^{2q}) integer points of norm about 2^q, gives Σ_{m≠0}|m|^{-3/2}(1+δ|m|)^{-N}≪δ^{-1/2} for N≥3. The error is therefore O(Rδ+√R δ^{-1/2})=O(R^{2/3}). All constants came from one fixed bump, the absolute ellipse-transform estimate and dimension-two Davenport; none depends on the form, aspect ratio, orientation or centre. This adapts the primary source’s smoothing argument with an isotropic bump instead of dropping its G₀,G₁ factors.
acceptance: A long thin ellipse is handled by B<2δ; its major semiaxis is then O(R^{1/3}).
All orientations are allowed: no integral rotation or bounded shape reduction occurs.
For E/a with area(E)≥a², R(E)/a≥1/√π, so the additive one can be absorbed uniformly.

sources.locator: §3 smoothing proof, (3.4), pp.4–5; Satz 2 proof, (3.18)–(3.20), pp.8–9
sources.match: The proof here adapts the explicit Fourier/smoothing argument, keeping a uniform curvature coefficient; it does not claim the source’s displayed G₀,G₁ bound already has the desired form.

nodes.title: Van der Corput's bound for C² convex domains
nodes.statement: For every fixed C² convex planar domain E with nonzero curvature there is C_E such that every real x≥1 satisfies |#(xE∩ℤ²)−x²area(E)|≤C_E x^{2/3}. For ellipses the stronger shape-uniform conclusion is uniform-ellipse-lattice-count, with the absolute curvature-dependent bound C(1+R_max(E))^{2/3}. In particular every θ>2/3 is admissible for integral binary forms.
hypotheses: The general C² assertion is a fixed-domain theorem. Its constant is not used to prove uniformity over changing ellipses.
The survey also reports Chaix’s stronger absolute-curvature form for general C² domains; its unseen primary proof is not claimed here.
proofSteps: For a fixed E split the boundary into finitely many graph arcs with bounded slope, interchanging the coordinate axes near vertical tangencies. The two curvature bounds of this fixed domain give positive E-dependent lower and upper bounds for the absolute second derivative on these arcs. Under dilation by x the bounds are proportional to x⁻¹.

The standard sawtooth-sum argument uses a Fourier cutoff H and the second-derivative estimate on each graph arc. Its bound is O_E(x/H+√(xH)+√x+1); taking H comparable to x^{1/3} gives O_E(x^{2/3}). Boundary-integral/Euler summation accounts for the graph endpoints and the area main term. This is the fixed-domain classical result reported in IKKN §3.1, p.9; the general primary proof remains an indirect-source item.

For the parameter-uniform conclusion use the separate, fully quantified uniform-ellipse-lattice-count and admissible-ellipse-exponents. No assertion that a fixed-domain constant depends only on R_max is used.

nodes.title: Huxley's bound for C³ convex domains
nodes.statement: Target contract: for every C³ convex planar domain E with nonzero curvature, |#(xE∩ℤ²)−x²area(E)|≤C_E x^{131/208}(log x)^{18637/8320} for x≥2. The stronger input needed for admissibility is: there is one absolute C such that every ellipse F satisfies |#(F∩ℤ²)−area(F)|≤C(1+R_max(F))^{131/208}(log(2+R_max(F)))^{18637/8320}. The second assertion is an explicit unresolved Huxley input, not a consequence of the first assertion with an unspecified C_E.
hypotheses: C³ boundary in the fixed-domain assertion. The uniform ellipse assertion quantifies over all eccentricities, orientations, centres and scales.

Both the advanced exponent-sum proof and the precise uniform primary-source hypotheses are retained in the inherited Huxley gap. The certified elementary alternative in this continuation is exponent 2/3.
proofSteps: The fixed-domain exponent is reported in IKKN §3.1, p.10, and KN (1.1), p.1. Its proof uses the discrete Hardy–Littlewood/Bombieri–Iwaniec–Huxley spacing arguments. The 2003 primary proof was not accessible in a permitted readable copy, so this continuation does not certify or redevelop it.

For uniform admissibility the stated second contract must be established from a quantitative primary theorem, including its normalized-derivative hypotheses for unbounded-eccentricity ellipses, or by a separate proof. A bound with C_E depending on the ellipse is insufficient. Record this as an open inherited input; subsequent use below exponent 2/3 is conditional on it.

nodes.title: Admissible lattice-count exponents for ellipses
nodes.statement: Every θ≥2/3 is admissible in the sense of curvature-lattice-class. Conditional on the explicitly stated uniform ellipse contract in huxley-planar-count, every θ>131/208 is admissible. The latter range retains the inherited Huxley proof gap.

No bounded-eccentricity reduction is assumed. The 2/3 route is established by the primary-source Fourier/smoothing adaptation; the improved Huxley route is conditional.
proofSteps: For F=a⁻¹(E−x₀), the semiaxes and maximal radius of curvature scale by a⁻¹. Its area is at least one, and for an ellipse area(F)=πAB≤πR(F)², so R(F)≥π^{-1/2}. Apply uniform-ellipse-lattice-count: (1+R)^{2/3}≤(1+√π)^{2/3}R^{2/3}. This proves admissibility at 2/3 itself, uniformly even for arbitrary real ellipses.
Use the corrected exponent-monotonicity API, with its π^{(θ′−θ)/2} constant adjustment, for every θ≥2/3.

If the uniform Huxley ellipse contract is supplied, let η=θ−131/208>0 and use (log(2+R))^{18637/8320}≪_η(1+R)^η. The same lower bound R≥π^{-1/2} absorbs the additive one, yielding C_θ R^θ. This implication is valid without claiming that the unresolved uniform contract has been proved.

θ=0.64 requires the explicitly unresolved uniform Huxley contract.
An arbitrarily eccentric integral ellipse remains inside the quantified 2/3 estimate.

nodes.title: Points of a Markoff level set with a fixed first coordinate
nodes.statement: Let a≥3 be an integer and K≥a³+3a². Put B=K−a², q=a²−4 and U=a²/(2√B). The number N_a(K) of integer a≤m≤n with a²+m²+n²+amn≤K equals (B/√q)log((√(a−2)+√(a+2))/2)−E_a(K)+O(√K+a²), with an absolute constant, where E_a(K)=(B/a)(U√(1+U²)+arsinh U−U²). More precisely, replacing E_a by E_a^exact=(a/2)√(B+qa²/4)+(B/√q)arsinh(a√q/(2√B))−(a+2)a²/4 gives error O(√K). Here E_a^exact=E_a−a²/2+O(a). If K<a³+3a² the count is zero. In the feasible range a≤K^{1/4}, E_a(K)≍a√K.
hypotheses: The feasible range is exactly a³+3a²≤K; it implies a≤K^{1/3}. The simplified strip correction is only asserted with error O(√K+a²).
proofSteps: The n interval at m has length F_a(m)=√(B+qm²/4)−(a+2)m/2, for a≤m≤M=√(B/(a+2)). It is nonempty exactly when m≤M. The function is decreasing and nonnegative there; summing integer column counts and comparing with its integral costs O(√K).
The integral from 0 to M is the displayed logarithmic sector term. The integral from 0 to a is E_a^exact, by the elementary antiderivative of √(B+qx²/4). Subtracting gives the sharper version.

E_a is instead the integral from 0 to a of √(B+a²x²/4)−ax/2. The linear terms differ by x, whose integral is a²/2. The square-root difference is nonnegative and at most Cx/a for a≥3, so its integral is O(a). This proves E_a^exact=E_a−a²/2+O(a), and the stated simplified error follows.
acceptance: a = 3, K large: the main term is log((1 + √5)/2)·(K − 9)/√5.

At K=a³+3a² the only pair is (a,a). The sector minus E_a equals −a²/2+O(a), so a uniform O(√K) error with the simplified E_a is impossible as a→∞. The additional O(a²) is necessary; the exact strip has zero area at this endpoint.

sources.match: The source omits the entire excluded strip (reviewed PAPER-GHOSH-SARNAK-22/E1). This review additionally distinguishes the exact antiderivative from its simplified asymptotic strip: the latter has error O(√K+a²), sufficient for the final sum.

nodes.title: Counting points in the Markoff fundamental sets
nodes.statement: Let R⁺(K) = #{(x₁, x₂, x₃) ∈ ℤ³ : 3 ≤ x₁ ≤ x₂ ≤ x₃, x₁² + x₂² + x₃² + x₁x₂x₃ ≤ K} and R⁻(K) = #{(x₁, x₂, x₃) ∈ ℤ³ : 3 ≤ x₁ ≤ x₂ ≤ x₃ ≤ x₁x₂/2, 1 ≤ x₁x₂x₃ − x₁² − x₂² − x₃² ≤ K}. Then R^±(K) = (1/48)K(log K)² + O(K log K).
hypotheses: The constant is 1/48 for both signs (corrected from the printed 1/36 for R⁺).
proofSteps: Sum markoff-fibre-count up to the largest feasible A(K), with a³+3a²≤K. Replacing A(K) by K^{1/3} changes only O(1) end slices and costs O(K log K). The sector main terms are (K/2)(log a)/a plus summable O(K/a) and O(a log a) errors. Their sum is K(log K)²/36+O(K log K). The corrected fibre errors sum to O(√K·K^{1/3}+Σ_{a≤K^{1/3}}a²)=O(K); thus they do not change the leading coefficient.

The strip corrections are O(a√K) for a ≤ K^{1/4} (in total Σ_{a≤K^{1/4}} a√K = O(K)) and (K/a)(log(a²/√K) + O(1)) for K^{1/4} ≤ a ≤ K^{1/3}; with u = log a their sum is K∫_{L/4}^{L/3}(2u − L/2)du + O(K log K) = K(log K)²/144 + O(K log K), L = log K. Hence R⁺(K) = K(log K)²(1/36 − 1/144) = K(log K)²/48 + O(K log K).

For R⁻ fix a=x_1 and use the wedge m≤n≤am/2. Write q_a(z)=az−1−z² for z=n/m. The area with 0≤m, q_a(n/m)m²≤B is (B/2)∫_1^{a/2}q_a(z)⁻¹dz=(B/√(a²−4))log((√(a−2)+√(a+2))/2). The portion with m<a is S_a(B)=(1/2)∫_1^{a/2}min(a²,B/q_a(z))dz. Take the difference of levels B=K+a² and B=a² (replacing the strict lower bound by 1 changes only boundary errors). On 1≤z≤a/2, q_a(z)⁻¹=(az)⁻¹+O(a⁻²+(az)⁻²); hence for B≥a³, S_a(B)=(B/a)log⁺(a²/√B)+O(B/a), while S_a(a²)=O(a log a). The allowed a are at most K^{1/3}+O(1), and their total lattice boundary error is O(Σ_a√(aK))=O(K). Summing the same strip term gives K(log K)²/144+O(K log K), so R⁻ has coefficient 1/36−1/144=1/48 as well.
acceptance: The two counts have the same main term.

sources.match: States R⁺(K) = (1/36)K(log K)² + O(K log K) and R⁻(K) = (1/48)K(log K)² + O(K log K); the reviewed extraction re-derived 1/48 for both (PAPER-GHOSH-SARNAK-22/E1, confirmed).

nodes.title: Restricted second-moment bound for pairs of representations
nodes.statement: There is an absolute C such that for K≥2 and an integer d≥1 satisfying 16d²≤K, the number of integer quadruples with s₁²+d t₂²=s₂²+d t₁², |s_j|≤√K and |t_j|≤√(K/d) is at most C(K/√d + K log K·τ(d)/d). This range includes d=a²−4 in the asymptotic regime of Ghosh–Sarnak §9: (log K)²<A≪_εK^ε and √A≤a≤A, for sufficiently large K. No assertion is made for all d≤K.
hypotheses: K is real, d a positive integer; the stated numerical restriction implies K≥16. The estimate includes zero coordinates and the zero representation.
The positive definite form x²+d y² is primitive of discriminant −D=−4d, which need not be fundamental.
proofSteps: The common value n lies in [0,2K]. Apart from n=0, the box count is bounded by w_D² Σ_{1≤n≤2K} r_g(n)², where g=x²+dy², r_g counts representations modulo the w_D≤6 automorphisms. Each orbit has exactly w_D elements for n>0, since a nonidentity orientation-preserving automorphism fixes no nonzero vector.

Use Toma Theorem 1 with β=2 and −D=D₀ f². Its main coefficient is absolutely bounded: the factors w_{D/e²} are at most six, u_{θ_e(g)}≥1, and Σ_{e|f}φ(f/e)/f=1. Consequently the main term is O(x/√D), uniformly in f and g.

Keep the full error: Σ_{e|f}(2^{ω(f/e)}/e)√(x/a_{θ_e(g)}) + τ(f²) + τ(D)(x log x/D + x/D^{3/4}). Here a_{θ_e(g)}≥1. The conductor sum is at most √x·τ(f²), because Σ_{e|f}2^{ω(f/e)}=τ(f²); also τ(f²)≤2f≤2√D.

Since D=4d≤√K and x=2K, √(xD)+√D ≪ x/√D. The elementary divisor bound τ(D)≪D^{1/4} absorbs xτ(D)/D^{3/4} into x/√D. It follows by separating the finitely many primes p<2^4 in the product τ(D)=∏(v_p(D)+1); their ratios to p^{v_p(D)/4} have finite suprema. Finally τ(4d)≤3τ(d). These estimates give the displayed bound, including the single n=0 tuple.

For the GS application, choose ε=1/16 in A≪_εK^ε. Then 4(a²−4)≤4A²≪K^{1/8}≤√K for sufficiently large K, uniformly for a≤A. In the second moment of R_d, interchanging the two t variables converts equality of s²−dt² into the positive-form pair equation; the sector bounds s≪√K,t≪√(K/d) only enlarge x and constants by absolute factors.
The deleted unrestricted statement fails for K=2 and prime d→∞: t₁=t₂=0 already supplies five solutions. Retain that test so no subsequent extension silently drops the parameter restriction.
acceptance: For d=1 and K≥16 this gives O(K log K), consistent with the sum-of-two-squares second moment.
The diagonal family t₁=t₂=0 has O(√K) elements, absorbed since d≤√K/4.
For d=a²−4 the discriminant −4d is often nonfundamental; the conductor formula is used without replacing d by its squarefree part.

Supplies the fundamental-discriminant result generalized by Toma; it alone is not used to assert the nonfundamental case.

nodes.title: Lattice points on a hyperplane in the positive orthant
nodes.statement: Let d ≥ 2, L = v + Λ ⊆ ℤ^d a translate of a full lattice Λ ⊆ ℤ^d by an integer vector, and a_1, …, a_d positive integers. There are k ≥ 1, s ∈ ℤ/k and r > 0 such that for every integer n ≥ 1, L′(n) = L ∩ {Σ a_i x_i = n} is empty unless n ≡ s mod k, and if n ≡ s mod k then #(L′(n) ∩ ℝ^d_{≥0}) = r·n^{d−1} + O_{d,L,a}(n^{d−2}).
hypotheses: All a_i > 0: with some a_i = 0 the count is infinite (PAPER-LIU-WOOD-ZUREICKBROWN-24/E8, confirmed); then the simplex {x ≥ 0, Σa_ix_i = n} is bounded.
proofSteps: The values Σ a_i x_i on L form a coset s + kℤ of a subgroup kℤ ⊆ ℤ (k = gcd of the a-values on Λ).
For n ≡ s mod k, L′(n) is a translate of the rank-(d − 1) lattice Λ ∩ {Σa_ix_i = 0} inside the hyperplane; the points with x ≥ 0 lie in the dilated simplex n·Δ, Δ = {x ≥ 0, Σa_ix_i = 1}.

Apply the fixed-lattice count with Lipschitz boundary (GlobalNumberFields Layer 3) or semialgebraic-family-lattice-count in the hyperplane: main term vol(nΔ)/det = r n^{d−1} with r = vol(Δ)/covol, error O(n^{d−2}).

nodes.title: Transference with Minkowski's constant
nodes.statement: Let L be a full lattice in an n-dimensional real inner-product space (n ≥ 1) with polar (inner dual) L*, λ_1 ≤ … ≤ λ_n the successive minima of L and λ*_1 ≤ … ≤ λ*_n those of L* for the closed unit ball B. Then 1 ≤ λ_iλ*_{n+1−i} ≤ c(n) for every i, with c(n) = 4ⁿ/vol(B)².
hypotheses: Euclidean ball on both sides; the constant is weaker than Banaszczyk's n (dual-transference-upper) but the proof is complete from Minkowski's second theorem.
proofSteps: Lower bound: dual-transference-lower (for every j, λ_jλ*_{n+1−j} ≥ 1).
Minkowski's second theorem for L and L* (GN.1 minkowski-second-upper) with covol(L)covol(L*) = 1 (GN.0 covolume-dual): ∏_j λ_j·∏_j λ*_j ≤ 4ⁿ/vol(B)².
Hence λ_iλ*_{n+1−i} = ∏_j(λ_jλ*_{n+1−j}) / ∏_{j≠i}(λ_jλ*_{n+1−j}) ≤ 4ⁿ/vol(B)², the denominator being ≥ 1.
acceptance: L = ℤⁿ: all minima are 1 and the products equal 1.

nodes.title: Covering from a lower bound on the dual lattice
nodes.statement: Let L be a full lattice in ℝⁿ (n ≥ 1) with polar L* = {y : ⟨y, x⟩ ∈ ℤ for all x ∈ L}, and R > 0. (a) If ‖y‖₂ ≥ R for every nonzero y ∈ L*, then every b ∈ ℝⁿ has some x ∈ L with ‖x − b‖₂ ≤ n/R. (b) If ‖y‖_∞ ≥ R for every nonzero y ∈ L*, then every b has some x ∈ L with ‖x − b‖_∞ ≤ ‖x − b‖₂ ≤ n/R. In terms of a basis matrix B (L = Bℤⁿ, L* = (Bᵀ)^{−1}ℤⁿ) the constant n depends only on n.
hypotheses: For the same numerical R, the sup-norm lower bound in (b) implies the Euclidean lower bound in (a), since ‖y‖₂ ≥ ‖y‖∞; hence (b) follows directly from (a).
proofSteps: (a) μ(L)·λ_1(L*) ≤ n (covering-dual-transference) and λ_1(L*) ≥ R give μ(L) ≤ n/R; the covering radius is attained (covering-radius).
(b) ‖y‖₂ ≥ ‖y‖_∞ ≥ R, so (a) applies; finally ‖x − b‖_∞ ≤ ‖x − b‖₂.
Evertse's Corollary 2.21 gives the same with constant n·c(n)/2 from transference-minkowski-constant, without Gaussian sums.
acceptance: L = ℤⁿ, R = 1: every b is within ‖·‖_∞-distance 1/2 ≤ n of ℤⁿ.
n = 1, L = aℤ, L* = a^{−1}ℤ, R = 1/a: distance a/2 ≤ a.

nodes.title: The minimum of a Construction A lattice
nodes.statement: Let p be prime, n ≥ 1, C ⊆ 𝔽_pⁿ a linear code and L_C = {x ∈ ℤⁿ : x mod p ∈ C} its unscaled Construction A lattice. For c ∈ C let wt_E(c) = Σ_i c̃_i², where c̃_i ∈ ℤ is the representative of c_i with |c̃_i| ≤ p/2 (the Euclidean weight). Then min{‖x‖² : x ∈ L_C ∖ {0}} = min(p², min_{c ∈ C∖{0}} wt_E(c)) (with the second term omitted for C = 0). For p = 2, wt_E is the Hamming weight, so the minimal norm is min(4, d(C)).
hypotheses: The real realisation is the one of construction-a-real-lattice-interface (scale 1); the rescaled lattice p^{−1/2}L_C has minimal norm divided by p.
proofSteps: If x ∈ L_C is nonzero with x ∈ pℤⁿ then ‖x‖² ≥ p², attained by pe_1.
Otherwise c = x mod p ≠ 0 and |x_i| ≥ |c̃_i| coordinatewise, so ‖x‖² ≥ wt_E(c); the lift (c̃_i) itself lies in L_C.
For p = 2, c̃_i ∈ {0, 1} and wt_E(c) = wt_H(c).
acceptance: C = 0: L_C = pℤⁿ and the minimal norm is p².
C = 𝔽_pⁿ: L_C = ℤⁿ and the minimum is 1 = wt_E(e_1).
The extended Hamming [8,4,4] code over 𝔽₂ gives minimal norm min(4, 4) = 4 (the E₈ lattice scaled by √2).

nodes.title: The space of unimodular lattices
nodes.statement: For n ≥ 1 let G_n = SL_n(ℝ) with its matrix topology and Γ_n = SL_n(ℤ), embedded in G_n by the entrywise cast. The space of unimodular lattices is X_n = G_n/Γ_n (left cosets gΓ_n) with the quotient topology and its Borel σ-algebra, with the continuous left action h·gΓ_n = hgΓ_n. The map gΓ_n ↦ gℤⁿ (the lattice spanned by the columns of g) is a bijection from X_n onto the set of full lattices in ℝⁿ of covolume 1, equivariant for the linear action of SL_n(ℝ). The right-coset model Γ_n\G_n (lattice spanned by the rows) is identified with X_n by Γ_ng ↦ gᵀΓ_n, a homeomorphism intertwining right multiplication by h with left multiplication by hᵀ.
hypotheses: n ≥ 1; X_1 is a point.
Column convention: g ↦ gℤⁿ; consumers in the row convention compose with the transpose homeomorphism.
The topology is the quotient topology; on lattices it is the topology of convergence of bases (Chabauty), which agrees with it.
proofSteps: G_n is a locally compact second countable topological group (closed embedding into matrices, Matrix.SpecialLinearGroup.isClosedEmbedding_val) and Γ_n is a discrete subgroup, so X_n is a locally compact Hausdorff space and the quotient map is open.

gℤⁿ = g'ℤⁿ iff g⁻¹g' ∈ GL_n(ℤ), and det g = det g' = 1 forces det(g⁻¹g') = 1, i.e. g⁻¹g' ∈ SL_n(ℤ), so the map is injective; it is surjective onto covolume-one lattices because every such lattice has a basis whose matrix has determinant +1 (change the sign of one basis vector if necessary).
Transpose: Γ_ng ↦ gᵀΓ_n is well defined since (γg)ᵀ = gᵀγᵀ and Γ_n is transpose-stable; it is a homeomorphism as transpose is continuous and involutive, and (gh)ᵀ = hᵀgᵀ gives the intertwining.
acceptance: X_2 is identified with the unit tangent bundle of the modular surface; the point Γ_2 corresponds to ℤ².
diag(t, t^{−1})ℤ² leaves every compact set as t → ∞ (mahler-compactness).

nodes.title: The invariant probability on the space of lattices
nodes.statement: For n ≥ 2 there is a unique SL_n(ℝ)-invariant Borel probability measure μ_n on X_n. It is the normalised pushforward of Haar measure restricted to a measurable fundamental domain: for a fundamental domain F of Γ_n in SL_n(ℝ), μ_n(A) = m_G(F ∩ π⁻¹A)/m_G(F), and m_G(F) < ∞ because Γ_n is a lattice.
hypotheses: n ≥ 2 (for n = 1 the space is a point and μ_1 is the Dirac mass).
Uniqueness is among invariant Borel probability measures on the homogeneous space; full Haar measure on G cannot be pushed forward and normalised, since Γ is infinite.
proofSteps: Use the homogeneous-space quotient integral formula of AdelicAlgebraicGroups AA.2 for the discrete, nonnormal subgroup Γ_n. The Mathlib quotient-group Haar theorem assumes a normal subgroup and is not a provider here.
Finite covolume: Siegel sets cover SL_n(ℝ) up to Γ_n and have finite Haar measure (AdelicAlgebraicGroups AA.3, 'S-arithmetic subgroups are lattices' with S = {∞}, or gln-real-reduction); normalise.

Uniqueness: a G-invariant Borel probability on G/Γ_n lifts, through a measurable fundamental domain, to a left-invariant Radon measure on G, i.e. a Haar measure, unique up to the scalar fixed by the total mass.
acceptance: μ_2 corresponds, under X_2 ≅ T¹(SL_2(ℤ)\ℍ), to the normalised Liouville measure; the hyperbolic area of the modular surface is π/3.

nodes.title: Mahler's criterion with the sup norm
nodes.statement: For n ≥ 2 and ε > 0 the set {x ∈ X_n : ‖v‖_∞ ≥ ε for every nonzero v ∈ toLattice x} is compact, and a subset of X_n is relatively compact iff the sup-norm first minimum is bounded below on it by a positive constant. The same holds with ‖·‖_∞ replaced by any norm on ℝⁿ.
hypotheses: The equivalence of norms changes ε by a factor depending only on n.
proofSteps: ‖v‖_∞ ≤ ‖v‖₂ ≤ √n‖v‖_∞, so the sup-norm set for ε lies between the Euclidean sets for ε and √n·ε.
Apply the Euclidean criterion (mahler-compactness); closedness of the sup-norm set follows from continuity of the sup-norm first minimum on X_n.

nodes.statement: For n ≥ 1 and ε > 0 there is A(n, ε) such that every full lattice L ⊆ ℝⁿ of covolume 1 with λ_1(L) ≥ ε has a ℤ-basis b_1, …, b_n with ‖b_j‖ ≤ A(n, ε) for all j; equivalently L = gℤⁿ with g ∈ SL_n(ℝ) of operator norm ≤ A and ‖g⁻¹‖ ≤ A'(n, ε).
hypotheses: Covolume exactly 1 (bounded covolume suffices with A depending on the bound).
proofSteps: Minkowski's second theorem: λ_1⋯λ_n ≤ 2ⁿ/V_n, so λ_n ≤ 2ⁿ/(V_n ε^{n−1}).
adapted-basis-coordinates (or GN.1 basis-from-minima) gives a basis with ‖b_j‖ ≤ jλ_j ≤ n·λ_n.
The inverse: the rows of g⁻¹ form the dual basis, whose norms are ≤ ∏_{i≠j}‖b_i‖/covol by Cramer and Hadamard.
