L = diag(ε, 1/ε)ℤ²: the basis (ε, 0), (0, 1/ε) has norm 1/ε, consistent with A(2, ε) ≥ 1/ε.

For n = 2, a_t = diag(e^t, e^{−t}), u_t = [[1, t], [0, 1]] and ū_t = [[1, 0], [t, 1]]; they satisfy a_s u_t a_{−s} = u_{e^{2s}t}. The time-one map of a is T(x) = a_1·x.

proofSteps: t ↦ a_t and t ↦ u_t are continuous homomorphisms ℝ → SL_n(ℝ) (matrix exponential), so they define continuous flows on X_n preserving μ_n.
The commutation relation is a matrix identity.

nodes.title: The Mautner phenomenon
nodes.statement: Let G be a Lie group, Γ a lattice and μ a probability measure on Γ\G invariant under one-parameter subgroups u_t and a_s with a_{−s}u_ta_s = u_{e^s t}. If f ∈ L²(Γ\G, μ) is essentially a_s-invariant then f is essentially u_t-invariant.
hypotheses: Only the commutation relation and invariance of μ under both flows are used.
proofSteps: The unitary operators U_t, A_s of right translation satisfy A_{−s}U_tA_s = U_{e^s t}.
If A_sf = f then ‖U_tf − f‖ = ‖A_{−s}U_tA_sf − f‖ = ‖U_{e^st}f − f‖ for all s; letting s → −∞ and using strong continuity of t ↦ U_t gives U_tf = f.
acceptance: G = SL(2, ℝ): the geodesic flow and horocycle flow satisfy the relation.

sources.match: States the Mautner phenomenon in this form, with the ergodicity consequences for the geodesic flow.

nodes.title: Mixing of noncompact one-parameter flows
nodes.statement: Let G be a connected simple Lie group with finite centre, Γ a lattice, μ the G-invariant probability measure on Γ\G, and g_t a one-parameter subgroup whose closure is not compact. Then for all real-valued φ, ψ ∈ L²(Γ\G, μ): ∫ φ(xg_t)ψ(x) dμ(x) → (∫φ dμ)(∫ψ dμ) as t → ∞. In particular g_t is mixing and ergodic, and so is every time-t₀ map x ↦ xg_{t₀} with t₀ ≠ 0.
hypotheses: The limit is the product of the integrals, not of the L² norms (sourceIssue E402).
G simple (not merely semisimple): for products one must leave every compact set in each factor.
proofSteps: Use the base packet’s exact howe-moore-mixing contract: connected noncompact almost-simple real Lie group with finite centre, strongly continuous unitary representation, no nonzero invariant vectors, and escape from all compact subsets. Its general decay proof remains the base packet’s explicit gap; this continuation supplies the homogeneous-space adapter and does not assert a new contracting-subgroup generation theorem.

Right translation is unitary on L²(Γ\G,μ) by invariance. It is strongly continuous: continuous compactly supported functions are dense for the Radon finite quotient measure; translations converge uniformly on one compact neighborhood of their supports, hence in L². Approximate an arbitrary L² vector and use unitarity to pass continuity to it.

The invariant vectors are the constants. To justify the almost-everywhere point: smooth an invariant L² vector by a smooth compactly supported approximate identity on G. In quotient coordinate charts differentiation under this compact convolution gives a smooth representative, which is continuous and invariant; transitivity of G on Γ\G makes it constant. The approximate identity converges in L² by strong continuity. Thus the zero-mean closed subspace has no nonzero invariant vector.

A one-parameter subgroup with noncompact closure escapes every compact set as |t|→∞. Apply Ad, whose kernel is the finite centre and whose map onto the adjoint group is proper. For exp(t·ad X), a nonzero real part of an eigenvalue or a nonzero nilpotent part in real Jordan form forces its matrix or inverse norm to tend to infinity. Otherwise ad X is semisimple with purely imaginary spectrum and the closure is compact, contrary to the hypothesis. This also justifies both signs of t₀.

Remove the means of φ,ψ and apply the base Howe–Moore theorem to their matrix coefficient. Add the constants back to get the product of integrals. For complex functions the sesquilinear version uses conjugation on ψ and on its integral. Restrict to t=m t₀ with m→∞ (and the negative-time version when t₀<0) for mixing of each nonzero time map; mixing implies ergodicity.
acceptance: G = SL(2, ℝ), Γ = SL(2, ℤ), g_t = diag(e^{t/2}, e^{−t/2}): the geodesic flow on the modular surface is mixing.
For φ = ψ = 1_A with 0 < μ(A) < 1 the limit is μ(A)², not μ(A).

sources.locator: Remark 3.2.8, Theorem 3.2.9, Remarks 3.2.10–3.2.12 and proof, printed pp.103–105 (arXiv:math/0310402)
sources.match: States and proves mixing of one-parameter subgroups with noncompact closure on finite-volume quotients of connected simple Lie groups with finite centre; the displayed limit is misprinted as ‖φ‖₂‖ψ‖₂ (E402).

nodes.title: Mixing of the time-one map of the diagonal flow on X_2
nodes.statement: Let T : X_2 → X_2 be x ↦ a_1·x with a_1 = diag(e, e^{−1}). Then T preserves μ_2, is mixing (μ(T^{−k}A ∩ B) → μ(A)μ(B) for all Borel A, B) and hence ergodic.
hypotheses: Left action in the column convention; the row-convention statement for x ↦ x·a_1 on Γ\G follows through the transpose homeomorphism.
proofSteps: Transport to the right quotient by space-of-unimodular-lattices (transposeHomeomorph); there a_1 acts by right multiplication by a_1ᵀ = a_1.
SL(2, ℝ) is connected and simple with centre {±1} and {a_t} has noncompact closure; apply homogeneous-mixing with t ∈ ℕ to indicator functions.
Mixing implies ergodicity (if T⁻¹A = A then μ(A) = μ(A)²).
acceptance: Continuous-flow ergodicity alone would not give ergodicity of T; mixing does.

sources.match: Mixing of one-parameter subgroups with noncompact closure, applied to the geodesic flow on Γ\SL(2, ℝ).

nodes.title: (C, α)-good functions
nodes.statement: Let V ⊆ ℝ^d and C, α > 0. A continuous f : V → ℝ is (C, α)-good on V if for every open ball B ⊆ V and every ε > 0: |{x ∈ B : |f(x)| < ε}| ≤ C·(ε/‖f‖_B)^α·|B|, where ‖f‖_B = sup_B |f| and |·| is Lebesgue measure (with the convention 1/0 = ∞, so the condition is empty when f vanishes on B).
hypotheses: Continuity of f; balls are open Euclidean balls contained in V.

C > 0 and α > 0. In a real-valued Lean predicate use witnessed positive lower bounds M for sup_B |f|, rather than an unbounded real iSup; require the inequality for every such M. This agrees with the source on bounded balls by approximation to the supremum and also handles unbounded f.
proofSteps: Closure properties: |f| and λf are (C, α)-good when f is; sup_{i∈I}|f_i| is (C, α)-good when every f_i is.

Polynomials: a real polynomial of degree ≤ k in one variable is (2k(k+1)^{1/k}, 1/k)-good on ℝ, by Lagrange interpolation at k + 1 well-separated points where |f| < ε. Here k ≥ 1; degree-zero polynomials can be included by choosing k = 1.

nodes.title: Marked points of a partially ordered family
nodes.statement: Let S be a partially ordered set, ψ_s:V→ℝ, and 0<ε≤ρ. A point x∈V is (ε,ρ)-marked if there is a finite chain Σ⊆S such that ε≤|ψ_s(x)|≤ρ for s∈Σ, and |ψ_s(x)|≥ρ for every s∈S\Σ comparable to every member of Σ. The empty chain is allowed; then the second clause tests every s∈S. Continuity is an additional hypothesis of the measure estimate, not of this pointwise predicate.
proofSteps: A finite chain and the two displayed inequalities are the complete data; the second clause also quantifies over elements when the chain is empty. No maximality condition is imposed on a marking chain.

For a singleton, a value below ε is unmarked and a value at least ε is marked.

nodes.title: Prescribed open intervals admit a cover of multiplicity two
nodes.statement: Let A⊆ℝ be bounded and prescribe a radius 0<r(x)≤R for each x∈A, where R>0. There is a countable T⊆A such that A⊆⋃_{x∈T}(x−r(x),x+r(x)) and every real point belongs to at most two selected intervals.
hypotheses: The chosen intervals retain their prescribed radii; covering their centres is sufficient. No assertion of two families with disjoint closed intervals is made.
proofSteps: Apply the pinned Besicovitch prescribed-ball theorem on ℝ with goodτ and multiplicity. Its finitely many families of disjoint closed balls cover the centres by open intervals. Each family is countable by assigning distinct rational points to disjoint nonempty open intervals. Thus the union is a countable subcover of finite pointwise multiplicity M.

Enumerate its triples of distinct intervals. At each step, if the triple is still present and has common intersection, remove an interval contained in the union of the other two. Such an interval exists: choose an interval with the leftmost left endpoint and one with the rightmost right endpoint; because the three overlap, these two cover the third. If one interval attains both extremes, it contains either other interval. Every finite step preserves the union.

Keep the intervals never removed. Each point belonged to only finitely many of the original intervals. If it lost coverage in the limit, the last removal among those finitely many would already have destroyed coverage at a finite step, a contradiction. Every surviving triple was processed and therefore cannot have common intersection. This proves pointwise multiplicity at most two, while retaining the prescribed intervals.
acceptance: One prescribed interval suffices for a singleton centre set.

For centres 0,1,2 and intervals (−1,1),(1/2,3/2),(1,3), all three are needed to cover the centres. Their open multiplicity is two, but the corresponding three closed intervals all meet at 1. This distinguishes the conclusion from the stronger two-color closed-disjoint-family claim.
Finite pointwise multiplicity of the initial cover is essential to the last-removal argument; arbitrary infinite redundant covers are not pruned without it.

sources.match: The one-dimensional recurrence uses covering constant two. This elementary adapter derives that open-cover contract from the exact prescribed-ball theorem at the pins; it is not a separate claim that KM proves Mathlib’s stronger closed-family statement.

nodes.title: Quantitative estimate for unmarked points
nodes.statement: Let d≥1, k≥0, B=B(x₀,r₀) with r₀>0 and B̃=B(x₀,3^k r₀). Let S be a countable partially ordered set, every finite chain of which has cardinality at most k, and continuous ψ_s:B̃→ℝ. Assume C,α,ρ>0, each ψ_s is (C,α)-good on B̃, sup_B|ψ_s|≥ρ for every s, and for each x∈B̃ the set {s:|ψ_s(x)|<ρ} is finite. For 0<ε≤ρ the measure of the unmarked subset of B is at most k C (3^d N_d)^k (ε/ρ)^α vol(B), for any prescribed-open-ball covering bound N_d as specified in the hypotheses.
hypotheses: N_d≥1 is any integer such that every family of prescribed positive-radius open balls, with bounded centres and radii bounded above, has a countable subfamily covering all its centres with pointwise multiplicity at most N_d. Pinned Mathlib supplies such a constant via its stronger finite-family closed-disjoint cover. In dimension one, interval-prescribed-ball-cover supplies N_1=2.
proofSteps: Countability ensures measurability: finite chains form a countable family, and each marking condition is a countable intersection/union of closed inequalities. The primitive-subgroup application is countable. For k=0 the poset is empty and all points are marked.

For an unmarked x∈B put H_x={s:|ψ_s(x)|<ρ}; it is finite and nonempty, since otherwise the empty chain marks x. For s∈H_x let r_{s,x} be the largest radius ≤2r₀ on which sup_{B(x,r)}|ψ_s|≤ρ. Continuity gives positivity and passage to the endpoint. Since B⊆B(x,2r₀) and sup_B≥ρ, the supremum at this maximal radius equals ρ. Choose s_x maximizing r_{s,x} over H_x and put B_x=B(x,r_{s_x,x}). Then |ψ_{s_x}|≤ρ on B_x, while sup_{B_x}|ψ_s|≥ρ for every s: for s outside H_x its centre value suffices, and for s∈H_x use maximality.

Let S_x be the strict link of s_x, namely all other elements comparable to s_x. Its chain length is at most k−1. The enlarged ball 3^{k−1}B_x lies in B̃ because its radius is ≤2·3^{k−1}r₀ and its centre is in B. All goodness, lower-bound and local-finiteness hypotheses pass to this link. By induction, its unmarked subset of B_x has measure at most (k−1)C(3^dN_d)^{k−1}(ε/ρ)^α vol(B_x).

If y∈B∩B_x is unmarked for S but marked for S_x, then |ψ_{s_x}(y)|<ε: otherwise adjoining s_x to a witness chain marks it for S (|ψ_{s_x}|≤ρ on B_x; any element comparable to the enlarged chain lies in S_x). Goodness bounds this additional set by C(ε/ρ)^α vol(B_x).

Apply the prescribed-open-ball covering contract to the balls B_x, centred in the bounded unmarked subset of B and with radii ≤2r₀. It gives a countable subcover of those centres with multiplicity ≤N_d. All chosen balls lie in 3B, so Tonelli gives Σvol(B_x)≤N_d vol(3B)=N_d3^d vol(B). Multiply the local bound to obtain kC(3^dN_d)^k, using 3^dN_d≥1. One available general-dimensional contract follows from pinned Besicovitch.exist_disjoint_covering_families with goodτ and multiplicity: each closed-disjoint family has countably many nonempty open balls by second countability. The interval adapter supplies a smaller constant for the weaker open-cover contract.
acceptance: k=0 gives zero unmarked measure.
A singleton poset reduces to the good-function sublevel estimate.
The finiteness assumption is pointwise, not a single global finite list of primitive subgroups.

sources.match: All length, goodness, nonvanishing and pointwise finiteness conditions are retained. The countable-poset specialization suffices for primitive subgroups and makes measurability explicit.

nodes.title: A marked primitive flag excludes short vectors
nodes.statement: For g∈GL_k(ℝ), k≥1, put ψ_Γ=‖g(v₁∧⋯∧v_r)‖∞ for each nonzero primitive subgroup Γ≤ℤ^k of rank r, independently of its integral basis. If 0<ε≤ρ≤1/k and g is (ε,ρ)-marked for the inclusion poset of such Γ, then every nonzero v∈ℤ^k satisfies ‖gv‖∞≥ε.
proofSteps: The exterior-coordinate norm satisfies ‖u∧w‖∞≤k‖u‖∞‖w‖∞ when w has rank one: each output coordinate is a sum of at most k products. If Γ is primitive of rank r and v lies outside its real span, Λ=(Γ+ℝv)∩ℤ^k contains Γ+ℤv with finite index. Basis wedges differ by that index, so ψ_Λ≤kψ_Γ‖gv‖∞. This is KM (5.1); no Euclidean-covolume substitution is made.

It suffices to test primitive v, since dividing out its positive integral content decreases its norm. Order a marking chain Γ₁<⋯<Γ_l. If v is in the real span of some Γ_i, take the first such i; otherwise use endpoint Γ_{l+1}=ℤ^k. Primitivity puts v inside that first Γ_i. Put Γ=Γ_{i−1} (or zero for i=1), and Λ=(Γ+ℝv)∩ℤ^k. The subgroup Λ lies between consecutive flag members (including endpoints), so it is comparable to the whole flag.

Thus ψ_Λ≥ε: either Λ belongs to the marking chain or its norm is ≥ρ by the second marking clause. If Γ is nonzero, ψ_Γ≤ρ, hence ε≤kρ‖gv‖∞≤‖gv‖∞. If Γ=0, do not use ψ_0=1≤ρ (false in general): Λ=ℤv for primitive v, so ψ_Λ=‖gv‖∞ directly.

For each fixed g, only finitely many primitive Γ have ψ_Γ<ρ. The integral basis wedge is a primitive nonzero integer point in one of the finitely many exterior powers; ∧^r g is invertible and a bounded norm ball contains finitely many integer points. The wedge determines Γ up to sign. The poset is countable and its chains have length at most k because proper inclusions of primitive subgroups increase rank.
acceptance: For k=1, marking forces the scalar |g|≥ε.
The rank-zero predecessor is treated by the vector norm itself; it is not bounded by ρ.
For g=diag(t,t⁻¹), 0<t<ε, no marking can exclude the subgroup ℤe₁, so the flag criterion correctly fails.

sources.match: The wedge norm, saturation and insertion of a primitive vector give the marked-point implication and pointwise finiteness.

nodes.title: Kleinbock–Margulis quantitative nondivergence
nodes.statement: Let d, k ≥ 1, r₀ > 0, C, α > 0, 0 < ρ ≤ 1/k, B = B(x₀, r₀) ⊆ ℝ^d a ball, B̃ = B(x₀, 3^k r₀) and h : B̃ → GL_k(ℝ) continuous. For a primitive subgroup Γ of ℤ^k let ψ_Γ(x) = ‖h(x)Γ‖ (the maximum absolute Plücker coordinate of a basis wedge of h(x)Γ, independent of the integral basis; this is not Euclidean covolume). Suppose that for every Γ: (i) ψ_Γ is (C, α)-good on B̃ and (ii) sup_B ψ_Γ ≥ ρ. Then for every 0 < ε ≤ ρ: |{x ∈ B : δ(h(x)ℤ^k) < ε}| ≤ k·C·(3^d N_d)^k·(ε/ρ)^α·|B|, where δ(Λ) is the sup norm of a shortest nonzero vector and N_d satisfies the prescribed-open-ball covering contract of marked-poset-measure-bound.
hypotheses: N_d≥1 is any integer such that every family of prescribed positive-radius open balls, with bounded centres and radii bounded above, has a countable subfamily covering all its centres with pointwise multiplicity at most N_d. Pinned Mathlib supplies such a constant via its stronger finite-family closed-disjoint cover. In dimension one, interval-prescribed-ball-cover supplies N_1=2.
Γ ranges over all nonzero primitive subgroups of ℤ^k.
proofSteps: Use the countable poset of nonzero primitive subgroups of ℤ^k, ordered by inclusion, and ψ_Γ(x) as the max absolute Plücker-coordinate norm. Basis invariance follows from determinant ±1 of a change of integral basis. Proper primitive inclusions increase rank, so chain length is at most k.

The finite-exterior-lattice argument in primitive-flag-short-vector proves pointwise finiteness below ρ for every x, even though no finite list works globally. Continuity of h makes every ψ_Γ continuous. The stated hypotheses are precisely the remaining assumptions of marked-poset-measure-bound.
Apply that estimate. By primitive-flag-short-vector and ρ≤1/k, every marked point has δ(h(x)ℤ^k)≥ε. Therefore the set with δ<ε is contained in the unmarked set, giving the claimed measure bound.
acceptance: k = 1: h(x) is a scalar and the statement is the good property of |h| itself.
Constant h(x) = g: the set is empty or all of B according as δ(gℤ^k) ≥ ε or not, consistent with (ii).

sources.locator: §4, Theorem 4.1 and proof, pp.9–13; §5, (5.1), Theorem 5.2 and proof, pp.13–15 (arXiv:math/9810036)
sources.match: States the measure bound k C (3^d N_d)^k (ε/ρ)^α |B| under hypotheses (i)–(ii) on the functions ψ_Γ.

nodes.title: Quantitative recurrence of unipotent trajectories
nodes.statement: For every lattice Λ ⊆ ℝ^k there is ρ = ρ(Λ) > 0 such that for every one-parameter unipotent subgroup {u_x} of SL_k(ℝ), every T > 0 and every 0 < ε ≤ ρ: |{0 < x < T : δ(u_xΛ) < ε}| ≤ 2k³·6^k·(k² + 1)^{1/k²}·(ε/ρ)^{1/k²}·T. Consequently, for every x₀ ∈ X_k and η > 0 there is a compact K ⊆ X_k with |{t ∈ [0, T] : u_t x₀ ∉ K}| ≤ ηT for all T > 0.
hypotheses: ρ depends on Λ (not on u or T); the compact set in the consequence is uniform in T, which strengthens base unipotent-nondivergence.
k ≥ 1 and 0 < ε ≤ ρ. The exact source constant uses sup norms for vectors and exterior powers; the same upper bound for the Euclidean short-vector event follows from ‖v‖∞ ≤ ‖v‖₂.
proofSteps: Write Λ = gℤ^k and h(x) = u_xg. For a primitive Γ with basis v_1, …, v_j the coordinates of h(x)(v_1 ∧ ⋯ ∧ v_j) are polynomials of degree ≤ k² in x, hence (2k²(k² + 1)^{1/k²}, 1/k²)-good (good-functions), and so is ψ_Γ.
ρ = min(1/k, inf_Γ ‖gΓ‖) > 0 by discreteness of Λ; ψ_Γ(0) ≥ ρ gives (ii) on (0, T).

Use interval-prescribed-ball-cover to supply N_1=2 to the generalized quantitative-nondivergence theorem. The source polynomial-goodness constant then gives k·[2k²(k²+1)^{1/k²}]·(3·2)^k=2k³6^k(k²+1)^{1/k²}. This does not identify Mathlib’s closed-disjoint-family multiplicity with two.
The consequence: choose ε with the bound ≤ η and K = {δ ≥ ε}, compact by mahler-compactness-sup-norm (Euclidean version).
acceptance: k = 2, Λ = ℤ², u_x = [[1, x],[0, 1]]: every nonzero vector (p + xq, q) of u_xℤ² has norm ≥ 1 (q ≠ 0 gives |q| ≥ 1, q = 0 gives |p| ≥ 1), so the exceptional set is empty for ε ≤ ρ = 1/2: the periodic horocycle through ℤ² never approaches the cusp.

The qualitative recurrence statement for unipotent flows on Γ\G.

nodes.title: Invariant projective probabilities for unipotent and positive hyperbolic maps
nodes.statement: Let V be a finite-dimensional real vector space and a∈GL(V) either unipotent or diagonalizable over ℝ with positive eigenvalues. Every a-invariant Borel probability on the real projective space P(V) gives full measure to the set of a-fixed lines. This fixed set is closed, so every line in the support is a-fixed.
proofSteps: For a unipotent, write a=1+N. For each nonzero v choose the largest j with N^jv≠0. The binomial expansion a^m v=Σ_i binom(m,i)N^i v shows [a^m v]→[N^jv], an a-fixed line, as m→∞.

For a positive diagonalizable a, decompose v into eigenspaces and take the largest eigenvalue with nonzero component. Dividing a^m v by that eigenvalue to the m-th power gives convergence in projective space to its component line, again fixed.

Poincaré recurrence for the invariant finite measure, applied to a countable basis of projective neighborhoods, gives almost every point a subsequence a^{m_i}[v]→[v]. The preceding full-orbit limit is a fixed line, hence [v] itself is fixed. Since the fixed-line set is closed, it contains the support. No claim that all vectors, rather than their lines, are fixed is used.
acceptance: For diag(2,1), an invariant probability is supported on its two eigenlines.
A scalar positive map fixes every line, so every probability is allowed.
A nontrivial rotation need not have a fixed real line and can preserve angular probability; the spectral hypothesis cannot be dropped.

sources.match: Finite invariant measure plus the projective asymptotic of unipotent/positive hyperbolic iterates forces support on fixed lines.

nodes.title: Borel's density theorem
nodes.statement: Let G be a closed subgroup of SL_ℓ(ℝ) and Γ a lattice in G (discrete with G/Γ of finite G-invariant measure). Then the Zariski closure of Γ in SL_ℓ(ℝ) (the common zero set of all polynomial functions in the matrix entries vanishing on Γ) contains every unipotent element and every hyperbolic (diagonalisable over ℝ with positive eigenvalues) element of G.
hypotheses: G closed in SL_ℓ(ℝ); no connectedness or semisimplicity is assumed in this form.
The conclusion concerns unipotent and hyperbolic elements, not all of G.
proofSteps: Let H be the algebraic Zariski closure of Γ in SL_ℓ. Multiplication and inversion are regular, so H is an algebraic subgroup. Import the existing Chevalley stabilizer theorem through ReductiveGroups Layer 3: there are a finite-dimensional algebraic representation ρ and a line ℓ with stabilizer H(ℝ). A single arbitrarily chosen polynomial vanishing on H does not have this property.

On G/Γ define F(gΓ)=ρ(g)ℓ. This is well-defined because Γ⊆H, is continuous and G-equivariant. Normalize the assumed finite nonzero invariant quotient measure and push it to P(V). The resulting probability ν is ρ(G)-invariant. The identity line ℓ is in its support: the preimage of every neighborhood of ℓ contains an open neighborhood of the identity coset, of positive quotient measure. Full support of the quotient probability follows from transitivity and second countability: countably many translates of any nonempty open set cover the quotient, so such an open set cannot have measure zero.

For a unipotent or positive real-hyperbolic g∈G, the ReductiveGroups Layer 4 contract makes ρ(g) unipotent or positive real-hyperbolic respectively. Apply projective-recurrence-fixed-lines to ν. Its support contains ℓ, so ρ(g) fixes ℓ and the exact stabilizer identity gives g∈H(ℝ).
acceptance: Γ = SL_ℓ(ℤ) in G = SL_ℓ(ℝ): Γ is Zariski dense.
A finite group Γ is a lattice only in a compact G, which has no nontrivial unipotent elements: consistent.

sources.locator: Proposition 4.7.1 and proof, printed pp.139–142 (arXiv:math/0310402), using Theorem 4.5.2 and Corollary 4.3.6
sources.match: States and proves that the Zariski closure of a lattice in a closed subgroup of SL(ℓ, ℝ) contains its unipotent and hyperbolic elements.
Uses Borel density: for a lattice Γ_S in a closed connected S, the real points of the Zariski closure of Γ_S contain the unipotents of S.

nodes.title: The five-dimensional so(2,1) quotient is the existing highest-weight-four module
nodes.statement: Let J represent Q(a,b,c)=b²−4ac on ℝ³, let 𝔥={A∈sl₃:AᵀJ+JA=0} and 𝔭={A∈sl₃:AᵀJ=JA}. Then sl₃=𝔥⊕𝔭 as 𝔥-modules, and the action of 𝔥 on 𝔭 is isomorphic to the standard highest-weight-four sl₂ module Sl2Std ℝ 4. Consequently 𝔭, equivalently sl₃/𝔥, is irreducible of dimension five.
proofSteps: Use J=[[0,0,−2],[0,1,0],[−2,0,0]]. The matrices E=[[0,1,0],[0,0,2],[0,0,0]], F=[[0,0,0],[2,0,0],[0,1,0]] and H=diag(2,0,−2) lie in 𝔥 and satisfy [H,E]=2E, [H,F]=−2F, [E,F]=H. They are independent and span 𝔥, identifying it with sl₂.

The involution A↦J⁻¹AᵀJ preserves trace. Its minus and plus eigenspaces on sl₃ are 𝔥 and 𝔭. Projection by one half of 1 minus/plus this involution proves the direct sum, and [𝔥,𝔭]⊆𝔭 follows by transposition. Directly solving the symmetric condition leaves six parameters and trace zero removes one, so dim 𝔭=5.

Put v₀=e₁₃ and v_i=(ad F)^i v₀ for 0≤i≤4. Matrix multiplication gives v_i∈𝔭, v_i≠0, [H,v_i]=(4−2i)v_i, [E,v_i]=i(5−i)v_{i−1} for i≥1, [E,v₀]=0 and [F,v₄]=0. Their distinct weights make them independent, hence a basis. Rescale the basis to the owner’s standard raising/lowering normalization to obtain an explicit intertwiner with Sl2Std ℝ 4.

Import irreducibility of that standard module from LieHighestWeight Layer 0, already implemented on current main. Transfer it across the intertwiner. A real change of coordinates and a nonzero scalar take b²−4ac to x₁²+x₂²−x₃² and transport the decomposition. This is a concrete adapter, not a new irreducibility theorem for general sl₂ modules.
acceptance: The five weights are 4,2,0,−2,−4, each once.
The plus eigenspace of A↦J⁻¹AᵀJ in all matrices has dimension six; trace zero is necessary to obtain dimension five.
Dimension alone does not imply irreducibility; the displayed nonzero ladder links all five weight spaces.

nodes.title: Connected subgroups between SO(2,1) and SL(3,ℝ)
nodes.statement: Let H = SO(Q₀)° ⊆ SL_3(ℝ) for Q₀ = x₁² + x₂² − x₃². The only connected Lie subgroups S of SL_3(ℝ) with H ⊆ S are S = H and S = SL_3(ℝ).
hypotheses: Connected subgroups; the statement is about Lie algebras 𝔥 ⊆ 𝔰 ⊆ 𝔰𝔩_3(ℝ).
proofSteps: Use so21-quotient-standard-module to split sl₃=𝔥⊕𝔭 with irreducible 𝔭. For any Lie subalgebra 𝔰 containing 𝔥, its elements’ 𝔥-components already lie in 𝔰, so 𝔰=𝔥⊕(𝔰∩𝔭). The latter intersection is 𝔥-invariant, hence either zero or all of 𝔭.

Therefore 𝔰=𝔥 or sl₃. The connected-Lie-subgroup correspondence from LieGroups Layer 2 identifies the connected analytic subgroup with that algebra; since SO(Q₀)° and SL₃(ℝ) are connected, these are the only choices. Closedness of the intermediate subgroup is not needed for the Lie-algebra argument.
acceptance: The Lie algebra 𝔰𝔬(2,1) has dimension 3 and 𝔰𝔩_3 dimension 8 = 3 + 5.

sources.match: Uses that a connected subgroup containing H = SO(2,1)° is H or SL(3, ℝ), as part of the proof via Ratner's orbit closure theorem.

nodes.title: Closed SO(Q) orbits come from rational forms
nodes.statement: Let Q = λQ₀∘g with g ∈ SL_3(ℝ), λ ≠ 0, and H = SO(Q₀)°. If the orbit H·gΓ_3 ⊆ X_3 (the lattices hgℤ³, h ∈ H) is closed and carries a finite H-invariant measure, then Q is a scalar multiple of a form with integer coefficients.
hypotheses: Q indefinite nondegenerate ternary; the closed orbit is the alternative left by Ratner's orbit closure theorem with S = H.
proofSteps: Closed finite-volume orbit ⇒ Γ_H = g⁻¹Hg ∩ SL_3(ℤ) is a lattice in g⁻¹Hg = SO(Q)° (Morris §1.1 exercises 22, 24).

Borel density implies that the Zariski closure of Γ_H contains the unipotents of SO(Q)°, which generate its identity component. Consequently every Γ_H-invariant polynomial form is SO(Q)°-invariant. Rational generators of the real Lie group are not assumed.

Consider the vector space W of ternary quadratic forms fixed by every γ∈Γ_H. Each invariance condition is a linear system with integer coefficients. Finite dimensionality lets finitely many of these equations cut out the same W, so W has a rational basis by Gaussian elimination. Its real points are fixed by the Zariski closure of Γ_H, hence by SO(Q)° from Borel density. After conjugating to b²−4ac, solving the invariance equations for the displayed E,F of so21-quotient-standard-module leaves precisely the line ℝQ. Thus W=ℝQ contains a nonzero rational form; clear denominators.
acceptance: For Q=x²+y²−3z² the invariance equations have integer coefficients and their common solution line is ℝQ; the adapter recovers its rational generator. Rationality is the conclusion being tested, not a proof here of the converse closed-orbit assertion.

sources.match: Shows that if the orbit closure is the H-orbit itself then the orbit is closed with finite volume, H ∩ gΓg⁻¹ is a lattice, and Borel density forces Q to be a multiple of an integral form.

nodes.title: Reduction of Oppenheim's theorem to three variables
nodes.statement: Let n ≥ 4 and Q a real nondegenerate indefinite quadratic form in n variables that is not a scalar multiple of a rational form. Then there is a rational 3-dimensional subspace W ⊆ ℚⁿ (with W ⊗ ℝ spanned by integer vectors) such that Q|_{W⊗ℝ} is nondegenerate, indefinite and not a scalar multiple of a rational form; restricting to W ∩ ℤⁿ ≅ ℤ³ gives Q(ℤⁿ) ⊇ Q|_W(ℤ³).
hypotheses: The subspace is rational, so W ∩ ℤⁿ is a lattice of rank 3.
Irrationality is not treated as an open condition; the proof retains an irrational ratio on two fixed integer vectors.
proofSteps: Integer vectors exist in both open sign cones by rational density. Suppose every pair of integer vectors v,w with Q(v)>0>Q(w) has Q(v)/Q(w) rational. Fix one such v₀,w₀. For any integer u, Q(u+mv₀)>0 for all sufficiently large integers m. Three consecutive such m give Q(u+mv₀)/Q(w₀) rational; quadratic interpolation at these integer arguments implies Q(u)/Q(w₀) rational. Evaluating at e_i and e_i+e_j then makes every coefficient of Q/Q(w₀) rational, a contradiction.

Choose integer v₁,v₂ with opposite signs and irrational Q(v₁)/Q(v₂). Their span is a nondegenerate indefinite plane: its Gram determinant is Q(v₁)Q(v₂)−B(v₁,v₂)²<0. Its orthogonal complement is nondegenerate. Choose a real v₃ whose orthogonal component has nonzero Q-value; nonvanishing of the three-dimensional Gram determinant is open, so rational density and denominator clearing give an integer v₃ with the same property.

The resulting rational ternary subspace is nondegenerate and indefinite. If its restriction were proportional to a rational form, the ratio Q(v₁)/Q(v₂) would be rational. Its integral intersection has rank three; the chosen independent integer vectors suffice for the asserted inclusion of value sets, even without choosing a saturated basis.
acceptance: n = 4, Q = x₁² + x₂² − √2x₃² + x₄²: W = span(e₁, e₂, e₃) works.

sources.locator: §1.2, proof printed p.14; Exercise 1.2#15 and its hint, printed p.18
sources.match: Asks for integer v₁,v₂ with negative irrational value ratio and a generic third vector. The proof above supplies the rational-ratio contradiction and nondegenerate extension explicitly.

nodes.title: The Siegel transform
nodes.statement: For n≥2 and measurable f:ℝⁿ→[0,∞], define Sf(x)=Σ_{v∈toLattice(x)∖{0}}f(v) and S*f(x)=Σ_{v primitive in toLattice(x)}f(v), where v is primitive in L if v∉mL for every integer m≥2. Then Sf=Σ_{m≥1}S*(f∘(m·)). For a measurable complex f use the same sums on lattices where Σ|f(v)|<∞, and set them to zero on the nonsummable set. The mean-value theorem proves absolute summability almost everywhere for f∈L¹, so this convention supplies its measurable L¹ extension.
hypotheses: The origin is excluded; for f ≥ 0 the transforms take values in [0, ∞].
Primitivity is in the lattice toLattice(x), not in ℤⁿ.

Order and nonnegative tsum identities in the API concern the [0,∞]-valued transforms. Complex reindexing identities hold wherever the corresponding absolute sums converge, hence almost everywhere for L¹ inputs.
proofSteps: Well defined on X_n since it depends only on the lattice gℤⁿ.
Every nonzero lattice vector is uniquely m·w with m ≥ 1 and w primitive, giving S f = Σ_m S*(f(m·)).
acceptance: S 1_{B̄(T)} counts the nonzero lattice points in the ball of radius T.
For f compactly supported away from 0 and x in a compact set, S f(x) is a finite sum.

nodes.title: Unfolding the primitive Siegel transform
nodes.statement: Let n ≥ 2, G = SL_n(ℝ), Γ = SL_n(ℤ), P ⊆ G the stabiliser of e_n (the mirabolic subgroup) and m_G a Haar measure. For f : ℝⁿ → [0, ∞] measurable: ∫_{G/Γ} S*f dm_{G/Γ} = c·∫_{ℝⁿ} f(x) dx, where c = m_{P/(P∩Γ)}(P/(P∩Γ)) for the compatible Haar measures on P and on G/P ≅ ℝⁿ ∖ {0} (normalised to Lebesgue measure); in particular c < ∞ and does not depend on f.
hypotheses: Tonelli for nonnegative f: no integrability hypothesis.
The constant c is finite because P ∩ Γ ≅ SL_{n−1}(ℤ) ⋉ ℤ^{n−1} is a lattice in P ≅ SL_{n−1}(ℝ) ⋉ ℝ^{n−1}.
proofSteps: Γ acts transitively on primitive vectors of ℤⁿ with stabiliser of e_n equal to P ∩ Γ, so S*f(gΓ) = Σ_{γ ∈ Γ/(P∩Γ)} f(gγe_n).

Unfold the nonnegative sum over Γ/(Γ∩P) by Tonelli and the AA.2 quotient integral formula, obtaining ∫_{G/(Γ∩P)}F for F(g)=f(ge_n). The pinned integral_eq_integral_automorphize is an integrable Bochner prototype for a countable subgroup, not by itself this nonnegative fibre formula. Then apply AA.2 again to integrate over P/(Γ∩P) above G/P. AA.3 supplies the finite mirabolic covolume. With Lebesgue-normalized measure on G/P this is exactly c∫f.
G/P ≅ ℝⁿ ∖ {0} via g ↦ ge_n, and the G-invariant measure on it is a multiple of Lebesgue measure (invariant-measures-punctured-space); absorb the multiple into c.
acceptance: n = 2: the stabiliser of e₂ in SL₂(ℤ) is {[[1, 0],[k, 1]] : k ∈ ℤ} and P = {[[1, 0],[t, 1]] : t ∈ ℝ}, so P/(P ∩ Γ) is a circle.

nodes.title: Invariant measures on the punctured space
nodes.statement: For n ≥ 2, every SL_n(ℝ)-invariant Radon measure on ℝⁿ ∖ {0} is a nonnegative multiple of Lebesgue measure.
hypotheses: n ≥ 2 makes the action transitive; for n = 1 the group is trivial.
proofSteps: SL_n(ℝ) acts transitively on ℝⁿ ∖ {0} with stabiliser P (the mirabolic subgroup), so ℝⁿ ∖ {0} ≅ G/P; Lebesgue measure is G-invariant since det = 1.

An invariant Radon measure on a homogeneous space G/P, when one exists, is unique up to a scalar (it lifts to a Haar measure of G through the quotient integral formula); so every invariant measure is c·Lebesgue.
acceptance: The Dirac mass at e_1 is not invariant; Lebesgue measure restricted to the punctured space is.

sources.locator: §4, Remark 2, printed p.11 (PDF p.5); §6, printed p.14 (PDF p.8)

nodes.title: Siegel's mean value theorem, primitive form
nodes.statement: For n ≥ 2 and f : ℝⁿ → [0, ∞] measurable, ∫_{X_n} S*f dμ_n = (1/ζ(n))·∫_{ℝⁿ} f(x) dx, and ∫_{X_n} S f dμ_n = ∫_{ℝⁿ} f(x) dx. For f ∈ L¹(ℝⁿ), S f is μ_n-integrable and the same identities hold.
hypotheses: μ_n is the invariant probability; the identities hold in [0, ∞] for f ≥ 0 and integrability of S f is a consequence, not a hypothesis.
proofSteps: primitive-siegel-unfolding gives ∫S*f dμ_n = c'·∫f for a constant c' ∈ [0, ∞) independent of f.
S f = Σ_m S*(f(m·)) and ∫f(mx)dx = m^{−n}∫f give ∫S f dμ_n = c'ζ(n)∫f.

Let f_T=1_{B̄(T)}/vol(B̄(T)). For each fixed lattice use a bounded basis fundamental parallelepiped of volume one: the cells based at lattice points in B̄(T) cover B̄(T−D) and lie in B̄(T+D), for a fixed cell diameter D. Volume comparison gives Sf_T(x)→1; ball-count-successive-minima alone is only an upper bound. For T≥1 that bound gives Sf_T≤C_n(1+Σ_{j<n}(λ_1⋯λ_j)⁻¹). To dominate each partial inverse product, take independent vectors v_i of lengths λ_i for λ_i≤1/n, and integer coefficients |m_i|≤⌊1/(nλ_i)⌋. Their distinct combinations have norm at most one and number ≥c_n∏_{λ_i≤1/n}λ_i⁻¹. Factors with λ_i>1/n contribute at most n each, so every partial inverse product is ≤C_n#(L∩B̄(1)). The latter equals 1+S1_{B̄(1)} and is integrable by the already finite unfolding constant and Σ_m m⁻ⁿ<∞ for n≥2. Dominated convergence now determines c′ζ(n)=1, without assuming the mean value formula in the domination step.

Apply the nonnegative identity first to |f|. Finite ∫|f| implies Σ|f(v)|<∞ for almost every lattice, and likewise for the primitive sum. Positive/negative parts of the real and imaginary parts then give the L¹ formulas; the exceptional zero-totalization convention does not change an integral.
acceptance: n = 2, f = 1_{B̄(T)}: the average number of nonzero lattice points of a random unimodular lattice in a disc of radius T is exactly πT², and of primitive ones πT²/ζ(2) = 6T²/π.

nodes.title: The packet of CM points of a negative discriminant
nodes.statement: Let D < 0 be a discriminant (D ≡ 0, 1 mod 4). For a positive definite integral binary form Q = [a, b, c] (a > 0) of discriminant b² − 4ac = D let z_Q = (−b + i√|D|)/(2a) ∈ ℍ, its CM point. z_{Q∘γ} = γ⁻¹·z_Q for γ ∈ SL₂(ℤ), so the classes of primitive forms of discriminant D give a finite set Λ_D of points of the modular curve SL₂(ℤ)\ℍ, of cardinality h(D), the number of proper classes; each point carries the weight 1/ω_Q, ω_Q the order of the stabiliser of z_Q in PSL₂(ℤ) (ω = 3, 2, 1 for D = −3, −4, D < −4). The normalised counting measure of the packet is ν_D = (Σ_Q 1/ω_Q)^{−1}Σ_Q ω_Q^{−1}δ_{z_Q}.
hypotheses: Primitive forms (gcd(a, b, c) = 1); for fundamental D every form of discriminant D is primitive.
Reduced representatives (|b| ≤ a ≤ c) give the points of Λ_D in the standard fundamental domain.
proofSteps: z_Q is the root in ℍ of Q(z, 1) = 0; the transformation law follows from Q(γ(x, y)) and the action of γ on the root.

Proper equivalence classes of forms correspond to SL₂(ℤ)-orbits of CM points of discriminant D; there are h(D) of them (finiteness of the form class number, TauCetiRoadmap IntegralLattices binary forms).
The stabiliser of z_Q in PSL₂(ℤ) is the image of the automorph group of Q, of order 3, 2 or 1.
acceptance: D = −4: Λ_D = {i} with ω = 2.
D = −20: h = 2; the reduced forms [1, 0, 5] and [2, 2, 3] give i√5 and (−1 + i√5)/2.

nodes.title: The oriented closed geodesic of an indefinite form
nodes.statement: Let D > 0 be a nonsquare discriminant and Q = [a, b, c] a primitive integral form of discriminant D. Its roots w = (−b + √D)/(2a) and w' = (−b − √D)/(2a) are the endpoints of the hyperbolic geodesic S_Q = {z ∈ ℍ : a|z|² + b Re z + c = 0}. Let γ_Q ∈ SL₂(ℤ) be the generator of the automorph group of Q with attracting fixed point w (pell-automorph). The oriented closed geodesic C_Q is the image in SL₂(ℤ)\ℍ of the arc of S_Q from z to γ_Qz, oriented from w' towards w; for a continuous SL₂(ℤ)-invariant function f, ∫_{C_Q} f ds is the integral along that arc (hyperbolic arclength), and for an invariant 1-form ω, ∫_{C_Q} ω the integral along the oriented arc. Both are independent of z ∈ S_Q and depend only on the proper class of Q; C_{nQ} = C_Q for n ∈ ℤ_{>0}.
hypotheses: Nonsquare D, so the roots are irrational and γ_Q is hyperbolic.
Orientation from w' to w, i.e. clockwise on S_Q when a > 0.
proofSteps: γ_Q fixes w and w' and preserves S_Q; it acts on S_Q as a translation towards its attracting fixed point w.
Changing z along S_Q changes the arc by a fundamental-domain shift of γ_Q, leaving integrals of invariant integrands unchanged; replacing Q by Q∘γ moves S_Q by γ⁻¹ and conjugates γ_Q.
acceptance: Q = [1, 0, −2] (D = 8): S_Q is the semicircle |z| = √2 and γ_Q = ±[[3, 4],[2, 3]] (t = 6, u = 2 with t² − 8u² = 4).

nodes.title: The length of a closed geodesic
nodes.statement: Let D > 0 be a nonsquare discriminant, Q primitive of discriminant D and (t, u) the solution of t² − Du² = 4 with t, u ≥ 1 minimal. Then the hyperbolic length of C_Q (the arc from z to γ_Qz) is 2 log ε_D with ε_D = (t + u√D)/2, independent of Q. The length is the translation length of the parametrised cycle; it is not halved when C_Q retraces itself (reciprocal classes).
hypotheses: Lengths are for the parametrised arc, counted with multiplicity.
proofSteps: γ_Q = ±[[(t − bu)/2, −cu], [au, (t + bu)/2]] has trace t (pell-automorph).
A hyperbolic element of trace t > 2 translates its axis by 2 arccosh(t/2) = 2 log((t + √(t² − 4))/2) = 2 log ε_D.

The reflected form [a, −b, c] has geodesic −S̄_Q (the mirror image in the imaginary axis).

nodes.title: Weyl sums of spherical harmonics over lattice points on spheres
nodes.statement: For n ≥ 1 let R_n = {m ∈ ℤ³ : |m|² = n} and r₃(n) = #R_n. For a harmonic polynomial u on ℝ³, homogeneous of degree ℓ, and n with r₃(n) > 0, the Weyl sum is W_u(n) = r₃(n)^{−1}Σ_{m∈R_n} u(m/√n). The theta series with harmonic coefficients is θ(z; u) = Σ_{m∈ℤ³} u(m)e^{2πiz|m|²}, z ∈ ℍ, whose n-th coefficient is a(n) = Σ_{m∈R_n}u(m) = n^{ℓ/2}r₃(n)W_u(n).
hypotheses: u harmonic (Δu = 0) and homogeneous; ℓ = 0 gives W_1(n) = 1.
In Lean harmonicWeylSum is totalised to 0 on an empty sphere; statements about counting probability measures assume n>0 and r₃(n)>0.
proofSteps: W_u(n) is the integral of u against the normalised counting measure of R_n/√n ⊆ S².
Homogeneity gives u(m) = n^{ℓ/2}u(m/√n) for m ∈ R_n, hence the coefficient identity.

θ(z; u) converges absolutely on ℍ (polynomial growth against Gaussian decay); its modularity of weight 3/2 + ℓ on Γ₀(4) is the theta input recorded in the base packet's tier-move gap (MetaplecticAutomorphicForms MP.7).
acceptance: u = x: W_u(n) = 0 for every n by the symmetry m ↦ −m.
u = x² − y²: W_u(n) = 0 by the symmetry swapping coordinates.

nodes.title: Weyl's criterion on the sphere
nodes.statement: Let σ be the normalised rotation-invariant measure on S² and (V_k) a sequence of nonempty finite multisets in S² with counting probability measures ν_k. Then ν_k → σ weakly iff for every ℓ ≥ 1 and every harmonic polynomial u homogeneous of degree ℓ, ν_k(u) → 0.
hypotheses: Weak convergence against continuous functions on S².
proofSteps: Harmonic decomposition is obtained degree by degree from Δ(|x|^{2j}h_m)=2j(2m+2j+1)|x|^{2j−2}h_m in three variables, for homogeneous harmonic h_m. The nonzero coefficients give a triangular induction decomposing each homogeneous polynomial as Σ_j|x|^{2j}h_{ℓ−2j}. On S² these restrictions therefore span all polynomial restrictions, which form a point-separating algebra and are uniformly dense by Stone–Weierstrass.

For homogeneous harmonic u of degree ℓ≥1, average u over rotations. Integrating its finitely many coefficients commutes with Δ, so the result is a harmonic rotation-invariant homogeneous polynomial. It is zero for odd ℓ; for even ℓ>0 it is c|x|^ℓ, whose Laplacian cℓ(ℓ+1)|x|^{ℓ−2} forces c=0. Rotation invariance of σ then gives ∫u dσ=0. This supplies the orthogonality-to-constants step explicitly.
Hence ν_k(f) → σ(f) for f in a dense subspace, and uniform boundedness of the ν_k extends this to C(S²).
acceptance: For n = 3·4^j the set R_n/√n consists of the 8 points (±1, ±1, ±1)/√3, and for the harmonic u = Σx_i⁴ − 3Σ_{i<j}x_i²x_j² one gets W_u(n) = −2/3 for every j: these n are not square-free and are excluded from Duke's theorem.
